articles.title: Rochdale foster carers recognised for supporting over 1,000 children
articles.excerpt: At an awards ceremony in Rochdale Town Hall, 34 foster families were honoured for their commitment to caring for vulnerable children, collectively fostering for 465 years.
articles.content_html:
Thirty-four foster families were honoured at the annual Foster Carer Celebration Awards held at Rochdale Town Hall, recognising their dedication to providing safe and nurturing homes for vulnerable children. Collectively, these families have fostered for an impressive 465 years, supporting over 1,020 children and young people from newborns to 18 years old.

Among those celebrated were Michael and Marilyn, a couple from Milnrow, who have fostered for 50 years since 1976. They have cared for over 330 children, primarily focusing on newborns and siblings. Marilyn expressed her love for fostering, stating, "How long is a piece of string?" when asked how long they would continue. She reflected on the joy of seeing children grow up and receiving letters from adoptive parents thanking them for their influence.

The event highlighted the vital role foster families play in the community, providing stability and care to those in need. The awards serve not only to recognise the individual contributions of these families but also to raise awareness about the importance of fostering in Rochdale.

This recognition is significant as it underscores the ongoing need for foster carers in the area. With many children still in need of stable homes, the event aims to inspire others in the community to consider fostering. For those interested in becoming foster carers, further information can be obtained from the local authority's fostering service.

To accommodate various lifestyles and commitments, Rochdale Council, as part of Foster for Greater Manchester, also offers a number of different fostering arrangements from respite care to long-term fostering. People with the determination to make a positive impact in a young person’s life and who would like to find out more about fostering with Rochdale Borough Council, can visit the Foster for Greater Manchester website or call 0300 303 0321. The ceremony included heartfelt letters from adoptive parents, expressing gratitude for the care and support provided by the foster carers. These testimonials underscored the vital role that foster carers play in the community and the positive influence they have on the lives of children and families.

This recognition not only honours the individual foster carers but also raises awareness about the importance of fostering in Rochdale. The council encourages anyone interested in becoming a foster carer to reach out and learn more about the process, as there is always a need for dedicated individuals to provide loving homes for children.

articles.title: Bridge Street in Heywood closed over building safety concerns
articles.excerpt: GMFRS says firefighters attended for around two hours and 40 minutes after concerns about a building structure. The road's reopening remains unconfirmed.
articles.content_html:
Firefighters attended concerns about a building structure near Bridge Street in Heywood for around two hours and 40 minutes on Saturday 24 October, according to an updated GMFRS statement reported by the Bury Times.

Update: 12.55pm GMT, Sunday 25 October 2026

The fire service said one engine from Heywood was called at about 6.30pm on Saturday. Crews inspected the building and made the area safe alongside Greater Manchester Police and Rochdale Council.

The Bury Times also reported that police attended to help manage the cordon. Emergency services have not confirmed that the storm caused the structural concerns.

The reports reviewed do not confirm when Bridge Street reopened or provide information about injuries. The precise building has not been identified. The end of firefighters' attendance does not establish that the road reopened.

Earlier update: 11.31pm BST, Saturday 24 October 2026

The Manchester Evening News reported concerns that strong winds could cause a derelict building to collapse. Its 9.20pm BST update said the area had been made safe, the building was still standing and firefighters remained at the scene when that report was issued.

Earlier report: 9.25pm BST, Saturday 24 October 2026

the source reported that Bridge Street was closed by emergency services. Its photographs showed a police cordon, a marked police car blocking access and a fire engine.

Anyone encountering restrictions should follow directions from emergency services. Further confirmed information about the road will be added to this article.

articles.title: £150 off energy bills: Rochdale households urged to watch for important letter
articles.excerpt: Warm Home Discount confirmation letters are arriving for eligible households, with the £150 energy credit applied over the winter rather than paid to everyone at once.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale residents who qualify for £150 off their energy bills are being urged to check their post as Warm Home Discount confirmation letters begin arriving.

The government started issuing letters on Thursday, 22 October, with correspondence continuing through to January 2027.

Around six million households across Britain are expected to benefit this winter. The letters will explain whether the discount will be applied automatically or whether the recipient needs to provide more information.

Anyone whose letter asks them to contact the Warm Home Discount helpline must do so before 26 February 2027.

The Warm Home Discount supports eligible households, including people receiving qualifying means tested benefits. Eligibility depends on the scheme’s rules, including benefit entitlement and the electricity account arrangements on the qualifying date.

For this winter, the qualifying date was 23 August 2026.

The £150 is normally applied directly to an eligible household’s electricity account. It is not a cash payment into a bank account, and there is no single payment day for everyone in Rochdale.

Eligible customers should receive their discount by 31 March 2027. Residents can check their supplier’s app, online account or bill for the credit.

The scheme is separate from the Winter Fuel Payment and Cold Weather Payments. Receiving the Warm Home Discount does not affect either entitlement.

For households watching every pound, the important step is to read the letter carefully and respond if action is requested.

Have you received your letter or seen the £150 appear on your energy account? Tell us your supplier and experience in the comments, keeping account numbers and personal details private.

Scheme information: https://www.gov.uk/the-warm-home-discount-scheme

articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has collected £2.88 million from parking fines since 2023, with funds reinvested into local road infrastructure.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has reported a total of £2.88 million generated from parking fines over the last three years, according to data obtained through a Freedom of Information request. This figure represents an average of just under £1 million per year from 2023 to 2026, with the highest earnings recorded in 2025, amounting to £990,256.

In total, the council issued 90,644 parking charge notices (PCNs) during this period. The overall value of these notices exceeded £5.6 million; however, the actual income is lower due to successful challenges against fines and the costs associated with enforcement. The council has stated that all revenue from PCNs is reinvested into the local road network, which may include repairs to potholes, repainting road markings, and funding larger infrastructure projects.

The council emphasised that PCNs are issued not only for revenue generation but also for safety reasons, such as ensuring adequate space for wheelchair users on pavements and preventing blind spots at junctions. The data also highlighted the busiest areas for parking fines, with Newgate, Yorkshire Street Central, and Oldham Road Central identified as the top hotspots for PCNs issued.

This financial strategy raises questions about the balance between enforcement and community needs, as residents may feel the impact of increased parking restrictions. As the council continues to reinvest these funds into local infrastructure, it remains to be seen how this will affect road safety and accessibility in Rochdale. Readers are encouraged to share their thoughts on parking regulations and their impact on the community.

articles.title: M6 Theatre receives £73,500 funding for 50th anniversary project
articles.excerpt: M6 Theatre in Rochdale has been awarded £73,500 to support its 50th anniversary project, which will include community outreach and an interactive exhibition.
articles.content_html:
M6 Theatre, a prominent institution in Rochdale, has been awarded £73,500 to fund its upcoming 50th anniversary project, set to take place in 2027. This funding will support a range of initiatives aimed at celebrating the theatre's rich history and its impact on the community over the past five decades.

The anniversary project will feature an interactive exhibition and a digital archive, allowing audiences to engage with the theatre's legacy. Additionally, M6 Theatre plans to conduct community outreach projects that will collect stories from individuals who have been involved with the theatre throughout its history. This initiative aims to highlight the journeys of both audiences and theatre professionals.

Founded in 1977, M6 Theatre has made a significant impact on the lives of over 500,000 children and young people through its touring theatre productions. The anniversary celebrations will include a new youth theatre show, a community gala, and the commissioning of a specially made film and poem, all designed to enhance public accessibility and involvement.

The project will unfold over the course of one year, culminating in a celebration of M6 Theatre's contributions to the arts and education in the region. This funding not only marks a significant investment in the arts but also underscores the importance of community engagement in preserving local cultural heritage.

articles.title: East Lancashire Railway steam gala draws more than 2,000 passengers as numbers rise 21.4 per cent
articles.excerpt: Four visiting engines, late trains and a tribute to preservation pioneer Richard Greenwood marked a busy autumn gala on the heritage railway serving Heywood.
articles.content_html:
More than 2,000 passengers visited East Lancashire Railway's Autumn Steam Gala as four visiting locomotives helped deliver a 21.4 per cent increase in passenger numbers on last year's event, according to the railway.

The heritage line, which serves Heywood, held the gala from 16 to 18 October. Three of the four visiting engines were making their first appearances on the ELR, with autumn colours along the Irwell Valley providing the backdrop to a packed weekend of passenger trains, goods workings and late evening journeys.

A first visit from the Bluebell Railway

One of the headline visitors was South Eastern & Chatham Railway Class O1 No. 65, which travelled from the Bluebell Railway for what the ELR described as its furthest ever visit north.

Built at Ashford in 1896 and rebuilt into its present form in 1908, No. 65 appeared in ornate green SECR Wainwright goods livery. It joined resident Lancashire & Yorkshire engines 1300 and 752 in marking significant anniversaries connected with 1896.

Both resident engines received fresh paintwork in lined Lancashire & Yorkshire livery for the gala. No. 1300's finishing touches were completed the day before the event by the railway's resident Heritage Painters team.

Last chance to ride behind visiting pannier tank

Great Western pannier tank No. 7714 arrived from the Severn Valley Railway, courtesy of the SVR Pannier Tank Fund. Built in Stoke-on-Trent by Kerr, Stuart & Co. in 1930, the engine faced south during the gala, giving photographers a different view of the line.

Photographic run pasts with the railway's goods train at Burrs Country Park raised £493 in cash donations. The ELR says passengers have a final opportunity to travel behind No. 7714 on 24 and 25 October before it returns to the West Midlands.

LSWR S15 No. 30506, owned by the Urie Locomotive Society and visiting from the Mid Hants Railway, returned to the ELR for the first time since the 1993 Festival of Steam. It is due to haul scheduled steam services on 31 October and 1 November, as well as taking part in a photographic charter.

The fourth visitor, Hudswell Clarke No. 1208, also made its ELR debut. Usually based at the Embsay & Bolton Abbey Railway and owned by Stephen Middleton, the industrial tank engine worked shuttles to Ramsbottom and paired with No. 65. It carried names from different stages of its working life, including Harold, Illingworth and Mitchell.

Remembering a preservation pioneer

Resident engines City of Wells, Standard 4MT No. 80097 and Lancashire & Yorkshire Pug No. 11243 also featured during the weekend.

Friday included a tribute to preservation pioneer Richard Greenwood, who died earlier this year. Engines 752 and City of Wells, both associated with his preservation work, ran together while his family and friends travelled in the Lancashire & Yorkshire Directors Saloon. The railway said his ashes were scattered into the firebox as the train departed.

Saturday's programme continued after dark, with brake van journeys behind visiting Southern engines, a rare trip into Rawtenstall's bay platform and late passenger workings.

More than 250 volunteer turns

The ELR said more than 250 volunteer turns were needed to deliver the weekend.

General manager Lee Kenny said: “These are results that everyone involved can take pride in. They reflect a great deal of work before the first train runs, throughout the weekend and after the last visitors have gone home.”

He thanked the crews, station teams, stewards, cleaners, catering staff and those responsible for preparing and maintaining the railway, alongside the small team organising the event.

“The gala depends on people across the railway working together, and we are very grateful for the effort and commitment that went into this year's event,” he said.

The railway said the passenger increase helped raise funds for ongoing preservation. Transport for No. 65 was supported by the East Lancashire Railway Preservation Society and a private individual.

What is coming next?

The Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day on 14 November is due to feature engines 752 and 1300 together on the steam service. Pug No. 11243 is also expected to offer short driver experiences around Bury Bolton Street station limits for a small fee. The Directors Saloon is due to offer another opportunity to travel.

The ELR has also announced provisional enthusiast event dates for 2027, when it will mark 40 years since reopening between Bury and Ramsbottom:

6 February: Winter Warmer Diesel Running Day.

19 February: Roch Valley L&Y Pug Railtour Anniversary, with brake van specials planned to mark 60 years since the final Whitworth branch railtours.

20 February: Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day.

12 to 14 March: Spring Steam Gala.

10 April: Lancashire & Yorkshire Running Day.

1 to 4 July: Summer Diesel Gala.

23 to 25 July: 40th Anniversary of the ELR Gala.

11 September: L&YR Running Day.

24 to 26 September: Autumn Diesel Gala.

15 to 17 October: Autumn Steam Gala.

6 November: L&YR Running Day.

These dates and locomotive appearances are provisional. Check the railway's latest information before travelling at https://www.eastlancsrailway.org.uk.

Anyone interested in volunteering can find details of departments and recruitment tours at https://www.elrps.co.uk/volunteering.

articles.title: Urgent appeal to find woman after suspected human tissue discovered in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Police fear a woman who may have recently given birth needs urgent medical attention after a discovery near Watkins Street and Charter Street, off Kingsway.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS | ONGOING AND DEVELOPING STORY. This report will be updated when further verified information becomes available.

Detectives are trying to find a woman who may need urgent medical attention after suspected human tissue was discovered off Kingsway in Rochdale.

Greater Manchester Police said evidence found near the junction of Watkins Street and Charter Street suggests a woman may have recently given birth. Officers were called shortly before 9am on Thursday 22 October.

Police have been examining the scene and carrying out enquiries. Their priority is to find the woman and make sure she is safe and well.

Detective Inspector Daniel Daly, from GMP's Rochdale CID, said: “She may be in need of urgent medical attention, and she is our absolute priority at the moment - that is why we are asking anyone with information to contact us.”

Anyone with information, or who may have seen a woman in distress, should call 101 and quote incident number 684 of 22/10/2026.

Information can also be reported online or through GMP's LiveChat service at https://www.gmp.police.uk. Alternatively, contact Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

DI Daly asked the public not to speculate: “We would ask that people don't speculate on the circumstances of this discovery as it hinders our investigation and is upsetting for those involved.”

The information in this report comes from Greater Manchester Police's appeal issued on 22 October 2026. Police have not confirmed further circumstances in that appeal.

articles.excerpt: Police are seeking help from the public to locate Sean, a 22-year-old man who went missing in Rochdale's Milkstone area on October 20. Family members describe his disappearance as unusual and urge anyone with information to come forward.
articles.content_html:
Police in Rochdale have launched an urgent appeal for information regarding the whereabouts of a 22-year-old man named Sean, who has gone missing. He was last seen in the Milkstone area of Rochdale town centre at approximately 7am on October 20, 2026.

Sean is described as white, with a slim build, standing around 5ft 9in tall. He has dark hair and a thick moustache. At the time of his disappearance, he was wearing a distinctive black Moncler jacket made from shiny material, a black bodywarmer, and black trousers.

Family members have expressed their concern, stating that Sean's disappearance is unusual for him. They are pleading with the public to share the appeal widely in hopes of locating him quickly. They have not provided a last name for Sean, but they are urging anyone who may have seen him or has information about his whereabouts to come forward.

Anyone with information about Sean's whereabouts is urged to contact Greater Manchester Police by calling 0161 856 8643 and quoting log number 110-211026. The police are keen to hear from anyone who may have seen him or has any information that could assist in locating him.

articles.title: Rochdale schools benefit from Tesco's Free Fruit and Veg programme
articles.excerpt: Schools across Greater Manchester, including those in Rochdale, received over 750,000 portions of fruit and vegetables through Tesco's initiative, promoting healthier eating among pupils.
articles.content_html:
Schools across Greater Manchester, including those in Rochdale, have received a total of 750,600 portions of fruit and vegetables as part of Tesco's Free Fruit & Veg for Schools programme. This initiative, now in its third year, aims to encourage healthier eating habits among children.

The produce, which weighed more than 60,000 kilograms, was distributed to schools throughout the region. Apples were the most popular choice, with approximately 221,000 portions consumed, followed by bananas at around 103,000 portions. Satsumas and clementines also featured prominently, with about 88,000 portions provided.

Since its launch, the programme has supplied nearly 20 million portions of fruit and vegetables across the UK, benefiting up to 186,000 pupils. According to a recent impact report, 98% of teachers reported that the initiative encouraged students to try a wider variety of fruits, while 94% noted improvements in student behaviour.

articles.excerpt: Rochdale takes gold and the Town and City Centre category title at the national RHS awards, hosted at Rochdale Town Hall.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale has won gold and been named Town and City Centre category winner at the RHS Britain in Bloom National Awards, with the celebrations taking place on home soil at Rochdale Town Hall.

The national recognition celebrates the work of Rochdale in Bloom and the people who care for the town’s public spaces throughout the year.

Volunteers, local businesses, Rochdale Town Centre BID and Rochdale Borough Council’s environmental management teams have all been credited in the announcement supplied to Rochdale Daily.

Their contribution goes beyond colourful planting. The announcement highlights community involvement, pride in the town and caring for nature as central to the achievement.

For those involved, winning the category as well as a gold award makes the result particularly special. Hosting this year’s national ceremony at Rochdale Town Hall added another reason to celebrate.

The award is a moment of national recognition for the collective effort behind Rochdale’s public spaces, and a chance to thank everyone whose time and work helped make it possible.

Image credit: Ella Marshall Three emerging Rochdale artists will receive free studio space, materials funding and support to develop work for a joint exhibition. Richard Street Studios and Breaking Barriers have named Alisha K., Madison Marcantonatos and Georgia Scholes as recipients of support funded by The Haworth Trust. Each artist will receive ten free days at Richard Street Studios, with the studio time valued at an estimated £1,200 per artist. The package also includes a materials budget and technical and marketing support. The scheme aims to help artists establish their practice in Rochdale. Parvez Qadir, artistic director at Breaking Barriers, said, “Rochdale has no shortage of creative talent. What it has lacked is the financial support for artists to take that talent seriously at the start of their careers.” Alisha K., who works with oil paint and pastel, said this would be her first opportunity to work in a professional studio alongside other artists. She said, “By the end, I hope to have pushed my practice further and created a body of work that reflects what I can do.” Multidisciplinary artist Madison Marcantonatos plans to explore nostalgia and her own experiences. She said, “Like many creatives, I’ve been caught up in commercial work, which has left little room for my own practice.” Collage and textile artist Georgia Scholes plans to make a large-scale textile banner celebrating Rochdale’s radical history. She said, “This funding gives me the time to develop my practice and build connections in a creative environment.” The artists’ work will be shown in a joint exhibition at Richard Street Studios in March 2027. evidence_sources.captured_text: Nine-year-old guitar virtuoso on verge of setting world record - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS Nine-year-old guitar virtuoso on verge of setting world record A nine-year-old rock guitar virtuoso who is on his way into the record books wants to inspire others to pick up an instrument. Adrian Abraham, from Middleton, only started playing the guitar about two years ago. Later this month, he is taking the Trinity College London Grade 8 Rock & Pop electric guitar examination — and could win a Guinness World Record in the process. Adrian loves heavy metal and picked up the guitar after hearing his father, Abraham Joseph, play the acoustic guitar. His favourite band is Iron Maiden and his favourite song to play is Eruption, by Van Halen. His Instagram page features dozens of videos chronicling his journey, including performances of hits by Metallica, Guns ‘n’ Roses, Queen, Deep Purple, Slipknot and System of a Down. The youngster said: “I saw my dad playing the guitar and I thought it really sounded cool, and then I wanted to give it a try. Adrian prepares for his first live performance. Image: adrian_jaams “So then I gave it a shot and I started going through acoustic at first and eventually went to electric.” Abraham added: “I used to play acoustic guitar and he used to sit down and listen. One day he told me he wanted to just hold the guitar to get the feel of it. “He took the guitar and he held a perfect cord. That’s the time I realised the guitar is the instrument for him. “His first guitar was a classic acoustic guitar which he played for about three months before it wasn’t enough for him and we had to upgrade to an electric. He is really progressing well. “I’ve been in choirs and I picked up the acoustic guitar when I was in college. It was just for fun and then I left it, but then when Adrian was born, I had this overwhelming feeling I should play something to him which would sound good. Music brings the out a real person. “But then he reached a point where he discovering grade eight. I can only teach him as much as basics of the guitar but the further grades, he picked it up himself.” With the help of a tutor, Adrian could now become the youngest person to pass the Grade 8 rock and pop guitar exam, setting a world record. He said: “I feel very excited and happy that I could be beating a world record, and I’m very happy that I got this far. If I beat it, I’m gonna be so overjoyed!” READ MORE: New drive to open car wash in town Adrian has been given a Marshall amplifier and Solar guitar by the manufacturers. Image: adrian_jaams While Adrian has to showcase a range of techniques for the exam, playing his favourite song is already a challenge for guitarists. With more than 200 beats per minute, it requires a tapping technique, using fingers from each hand, instead of picking or plucking. Adrian said: “My favourite song would be Eruption from Van Halen, and since I just really like the tapping pod and it just really gets me. It is the most-iconic tapping song in the world and it just sounds absolutely great.” The youngster’s ability has earned global attention, including endorsements from legendary music industry brands Marshall Amplifiers and Solar Guitars, which have supplied him with equipment to help his music journey. Following his exams, the natural outlet for Adrian’s talent would be playing in a band. Abraham said: “When people hear Adrian, a lot of them want him in a band, but by the time they see him, they’re like, he’s too little . . . his guitar is taller than him!” But Adrian is clear that music will be in his future. He said: “My dream would be to be the best guitarist in the world and be playing with famous bands and having fun with them too.” But playing the guitar has other benefits too. He added: “I usually just like it because it sounds good, it comes down my stress and it helps me play it and it helps me to just enjoy relax and play some good songs because usually most of the songs are heavy metal.” By sharing his journey on Instagram, Adrian and Abraham want to inspire others to do the same. Abraham said: “Like Adrian, you don’t have to wait to pick up a guitar. articles.title: Rochdale Council plans major investments and heritage restoration
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has announced significant investments in heritage restoration and community services, including plans for Hopwood Hall and Middleton's regeneration projects, aimed at boosting local economy and services.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has outlined a series of major investments aimed at revitalising the borough, with a focus on heritage restoration and community services. In a recent column, Councillor Neil Emmott highlighted the council's commitment to enhancing local infrastructure and supporting residents amid ongoing cost-of-living challenges.

A key development is the council's recent victory in the High Court regarding Hopwood Hall, a historic building in Middleton. The ruling provides clarity on the future of the site, which has seen over £1.6 million invested since 2017 by the council and Historic England. Plans for essential repairs and feasibility studies are underway, with the aim of restoring the hall to serve the community and preserve its historical significance.

In addition to Hopwood Hall, the council is advancing its regeneration plans for Middleton. The acquisition of Middleton Old Grammar School is expected to attract a new tenant by the end of the year, while the long-derelict Warwick Mill is also set for redevelopment, potentially including new housing. Furthermore, the transformation of the Middleton Scout Hut into a community venue is in progress, aimed at providing activities and training for young people.

These initiatives are part of a broader strategy to stimulate economic growth and create jobs across the borough. With banking and post office services returning to Middleton town centre in the new year, local leaders are optimistic about the positive impact these developments will have on the community.

articles.title: Court Rules on Ownership Dispute Over Hopwood Hall
articles.excerpt: A High Court ruling has denied Hopwood DePree's claim to ownership of Hopwood Hall, concluding that Rochdale Council acted fairly in its decision to end the exclusivity agreement.
articles.content_html:
A High Court in Manchester has ruled against Hopwood DePree in his bid to gain ownership of Hopwood Hall, a historic manor house in Rochdale. The ruling concluded that Rochdale Council acted fairly when it ended an exclusivity agreement with DePree, who is a descendant of the family that originally built the hall in the 1420s.

The two-day trial, which concluded on 20 October 2026, centred on DePree's claim that the council had reneged on an agreement allowing him to purchase the Grade II-listed property. The council had previously worked with DePree for seven years to facilitate repairs on the dilapidated site, which is now part of Hopwood Hall College. However, in November 2024, the council stated it would explore other options, citing a lack of a commercially viable business model from DePree.

Following the court's decision, DePree expressed disappointment, stating that the ruling was a significant setback for both his family and the community. He indicated that he and his legal team are considering their options moving forward, while also pledging to monitor the council's efforts to restore the hall for public benefit.

Hopwood Hall has a rich history, having been owned by the Hopwood family until 1922, after which it changed hands several times and fell into disrepair. The council acquired the property in the 1980s and has since been responsible for its maintenance.

articles.title: Fireworks distributor with Rochdale premises fined £40,000 as fire service takes enforcement action
articles.excerpt: GMFRS has announced prosecutions over fireworks storage and licensing breaches, including a £40,000 fine for Boom Fireworks, which operates premises in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
A national fireworks distributor operating premises in Rochdale has been fined £40,000 following an investigation by Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service.

GMFRS announced prosecutions involving Boom Fireworks Limited and two Greater Manchester retailers after inspectors uncovered fireworks storage and licensing offences.

According to the fire service, Boom Fireworks operates distribution premises in Cheetham Hill and Rochdale. Its director, Hashum Malik, pleaded guilty to storage offences at Manchester Magistrates’ Court on October 6.

Inspectors discovered higher-risk Hazard Type 3 fireworks being stored contrary to licensing requirements. The stock was detained and removed, and the company received a £40,000 fine, alongside a surcharge and prosecution costs.

Separate cases concerned The Vape Store on Hollins Road in Oldham and Wise Buys on Bury Road in Bolton.

The Oldham shopkeeper received a suspended prison sentence after fireworks were stored and sold despite an expired licence. The Bolton shopkeeper received rehabilitation requirements and a curfew after inspectors found fireworks stored and sold without a valid licence. Courts ordered the seized fireworks destroyed.

What this means for late-night fireworks

For Rochdale residents disturbed by repeated late-night fireworks, the announcement highlights enforcement against businesses supplying and storing explosive products.

However, the prosecutions concern storage and licensing offences. Their effect on fireworks nuisance in individual neighbourhoods has not been established.

The existing rules already prohibit setting off fireworks between 11pm and 7am on most nights. The exceptions are:

Bonfire Night: fireworks may be used until midnight.

New Year’s Eve, Diwali and Chinese New Year: the cut-off is 1am.

Midnight is therefore not the usual permitted finishing time: on ordinary nights, the restriction begins an hour earlier.

How to report persistent problems

Greater Manchester Police says irresponsible fireworks use can harm people and animals, damage property and create a serious fire risk.

Residents experiencing an ongoing problem can report fireworks-related antisocial behaviour through GMP: https://www.gmp.police.uk/advice/advice-and-information/asb/asb/antisocial-behaviour/fireworks/

The force also advises reporting retailers selling adult fireworks to under-18s to Trading Standards.

articles.title: East Middleton councillor questions parking charge warning after petrol station breakdown
articles.excerpt: Labour councillor Georgina Jacques says she was warned about a parking charge while waiting for the RAC after her car broke down on Oldham Road.
articles.content_html:
Labour councillor Georgina Jacques says she was warned she could face a parking charge while waiting for recovery after her car broke down at a petrol station on Oldham Road.

Councillor Jacques, who represents East Middleton on Rochdale Borough Council, described the incident in a public Facebook post, asking whether the business could charge her when her vehicle would not start.

Writing about the breakdown, she said:

“So I’ve broken down in Petrol station on Oldham Road.

“Yes another car that’s absolutely useless ”

She then described a conversation with a member of staff:

“Anyway the guy working there said, I am gunna get charged for parking when his boss comes, as hes saying I can’t stay waiting for RAC!!! I can’t move my car obviously as it won’t start ”

According to her account, the vehicle was beside the station’s tyre inflation equipment. She wrote:

“it’s at the tyre pumper upper so not really blocking anywhere.

“So is this legal does anyone know surly they can’t charge me for breaking down.”

Councillor Jacques said the RAC had given her an estimated arrival window between 9.30pm and 11.30pm.

The screenshot does not establish that a parking charge was subsequently issued, how much was allegedly proposed, or which parking conditions applied. The petrol station is not named in the post, and its account of the conversation is not available.

Could she actually be charged?

A private parking operator can issue a parking charge where it alleges that a driver breached the site’s parking conditions. That is a civil payment demand, rather than a criminal charge. Whether a demand would be enforceable in this particular case cannot be determined from the Facebook post alone. The signage, terms, circumstances of the breakdown and evidence of the recovery arrangements would matter.

However, a breakdown gives a motorist a strong reason to challenge a ticket issued while waiting for repairs or recovery. Citizens Advice specifically identifies being unable to move a broken-down vehicle as grounds for an appeal. That does not guarantee automatic cancellation, but it means a demand should not simply be assumed valid.

Independent parking appeals service POPLA also identifies evidence of a breakdown and a recovery callout as relevant when exceptional circumstances prevented a driver from complying with parking conditions.

Drivers in this situation should retain recovery booking messages, attendance records and photographs of the parking signs. The Competition and Markets Authority advises motorists to preserve evidence when a breakdown occurs and to challenge a disputed charge rather than ignore it.

For now, Councillor Jacques’s post establishes that she reported being warned about a possible charge. It does not establish that she received one or that any payment was legally owed.

Sources: Facebook post attributed to Councillor Georgina Jacques, screenshot supplied to Rochdale Daily; council profile: https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=7226; Citizens Advice: https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/law-and-courts/parking-tickets/when-to-appeal-a-parking-ticket/; POPLA: https://www.popla.co.uk/appeal-guide; CMA: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/parking-charges-cma-takes-action-to-drive-improvements-for-motorists

We hope Councillor Jacques is rescued promptly and back to her council duties in the morning—with her car feeling rather more cooperative.

articles.title: Bamford and Norden’s 450-home allocation: housing choice versus pressure on green space
articles.excerpt: The Bamford and Norden allocation envisages around 450 homes alongside improvements to sports and recreation facilities. Its development framework promotes family and affordable housing, but a framework does not establish a completed scheme, a housebuilder’s final layout or an affordable tenancy.
articles.content_html:
The Bamford and Norden allocation envisages around 450 homes alongside improvements to sports and recreation facilities. Its development framework promotes family and affordable housing, but a framework does not establish a completed scheme, a housebuilder’s final layout or an affordable tenancy.

Earlier consultation records document objections about the potential loss of playing fields and pressure on existing sports facilities. Those are recorded community concerns, not evidence that the final scheme necessarily removes those facilities. The council says facilities will be retained and improved through development contributions.

The affordability question remains open. No verified price list, rental schedule or final affordable allocation has been established for a detailed scheme. Describing homes as “high quality” says nothing about whether local households can pay for them.

Infrastructure assessment should address traffic on the surrounding roads, safe walking routes, schools, healthcare and the cumulative effect of other development. The framework’s view that a site is deliverable is not a substitute for funded mitigation attached to a permission.

Until a delivery programme is established, the 450 homes remain potential contributions over time. They should not be represented as homes built this year. A named builder has not been verified, so no builder’s legal history can responsibly be attached to this allocation.

Taylor Wimpey agreed CMA undertakings in 2021 to remove historic doubling ground-rent terms. Its separate 2025 information-sharing case ended through commitments without an infringement finding. Neither establishes the same issues at Foundry Fields.

articles.content_html:
RBH’s next Lower Falinge phase is reported to envisage 270 affordable-rented homes across two parcels, replacing 150 homes proposed for demolition. If implemented on that basis, the eventual net addition is around 120 homes, not 270.

The screening-stage proposal includes houses and apartments. It does not itself grant planning permission for the development. The current reference identified in reporting is OTH/2026/0781; final layouts and consent remain separate steps.

There is a directly relevant legal history. Claimants’ barristers reported that the council conceded a challenge to its earlier demolition prior approval over its EIA reasoning. The later October 2025 decision was reported as a refusal. This concerned the decision-making process and should not be recast as a finding of criminal misconduct by a builder.

RBH says regeneration is intended to create safe, warm family homes and has held resident consultation. Existing residents need clear rehousing commitments, costs and any opportunity to return. A temporary loss of homes before replacement is also important for borough-wide supply.

The regulator’s January 2026 judgement confirmed RBH’s G2 governance and V2 viability grades, recognising improvement while identifying risks. It did not assess consumer standards through that stability check.

The infrastructure test must consider the whole regeneration programme and its phases, including services during demolition and reconstruction, rather than treating every parcel as unrelated.

Tram access is a benefit, but it does not establish capacity in schools, GP services, sewers or the local road network. A phased remediation and infrastructure programme will be needed to show that the allocation can become a safe neighbourhood.

The potential 250 homes contribute to the long-term pipeline. They should not be counted as completed housing, nor allocated to an unverified developer’s legal record.

Social rent is governed by national rent policy; it should not be presented as a guaranteed percentage of every local private rent. A useful affordability assessment needs actual weekly rent, service charges, benefit eligibility and allocation arrangements.

The developer’s reported statement describes reuse of vacant brownfield land. The final plans need to establish accessible routes, parking, drainage and adequate capacity in local services. A small scheme can still have important effects on immediate neighbours.

There is documented landlord-history evidence worth treating fairly. In a separate 2026 Ombudsman determination, MSV was found responsible for maladministration over meal charges at another tenancy and ordered to refund £2,248.47; complaint handling was not found maladministrative. This is not a finding about the proposed Kirkholt homes.

The regulator’s 2026 review also records MSV’s C1 consumer and G1 governance grades, with V2 financial viability. Both the complaint finding and the wider regulatory context matter when assessing how future tenants will be treated.

If delivered as described, all 28 homes would contribute directly to rented affordable supply. The scheme’s exact costs and delivery date still need confirmation.

articles.title: Where Rochdale’s next homes are planned—and who can afford them
articles.excerpt: Our investigation examines 22 housing developments and regeneration plans across Rochdale borough: homes, prices, affordable tenure, land, school places, GP capacity and transport funding.
articles.content_html:
The homes are planned, but will Rochdale get the housing its residents need?

Rochdale’s housing pipeline spans large farmland neighbourhoods, former industrial and retail sites, and replacement of existing social housing. The schemes are at different stages. Allocated land, a committee resolution, a formal permission, a construction start and an occupied home are not interchangeable.

How many homes is Rochdale expected to deliver?

The council’s 2026 housing topic paper uses the adopted Places for Everyone requirement of 10,472 net additional homes in 2022–2039: 568 annually in 2022–2025, 616 in 2025–2030 and 632 in 2030–2039. It records 650 net additions in 2024/25, above that year’s 568 requirement. This is historical performance, not proof of delivery in 2026/27.

Does the pipeline meet the government’s target?

The answer is qualified. The 2025 land assessment identifies sufficient potential supply against the adopted plan benchmark, but availability forecasts do not guarantee completions. National housing need is a separate calculation, using housing stock and affordability. The current national framework was issued in August 2026; older council estimates of the revised need are not interchangeable with a freshly calculated October figure. The latest annual delivery, current standard-method calculation and appropriate land-supply buffer still need confirmation before claiming the borough meets every present national requirement.

Why affordable numbers matter

The May 2026 housing-needs assessment estimates a net annual affordable shortfall of 768 homes under a ten-year backlog-clearance model. That is an assessment of need, not a separate statutory annual building quota, and includes the role of existing stock. Appendix C contains the detailed calculation; its headline gross figures are internally inconsistent, so this series uses the consistent net figure. The distinction is essential: meeting an overall housing target does not automatically meet the needs of households who cannot afford market homes.

What does affordable mean?

Social Rent is set under government rent policy. Other affordable rental products are regulated or discounted against local rents. Shared ownership and discounted sale help eligible purchasers but still involve household costs. For each scheme, actual rent, purchase price, unowned-share rent, service charges, estate fees and eligibility are the useful affordability evidence. A marketing incentive or a claim that a property is cheaper than Manchester does not establish planning-defined affordability.

Green Belt and brownfield are different questions

Green Belt is a planning designation; greenfield and brownfield describe the land and its development history. Agricultural fields can have been removed from the Green Belt while remaining greenfield. Brownfield can also lie within Green Belt. The quarry’s restoration history and the precise development boundary matter. “Brown belt” is not the equivalent planning category.

Do stronger Green Belt affordable rules apply to these schemes?

Current policy GB8 includes affordable provision, infrastructure and accessible green space. Its footnote 43 excludes development on land released through plans adopted before 12 December 2024, and permissions on Green Belt granted before that date. Places for Everyone was adopted in March 2024. It would therefore be misleading to say every listed former Green Belt allocation automatically requires 50% affordable housing. The actual site, date of release, permission and obligations must be checked.

Can infrastructure cope?

The August 2026 infrastructure document is a scoping assessment and coordination framework. It discusses assessment, funding and healthcare planning; it is not proof that every scheme already has funded school places, staffed GP capacity or completed drainage works. The defensible borough-wide conclusion is that support depends on scheme-specific evidence and delivery. This review does not establish that infrastructure either universally supports or universally fails the housing programme.

What evidence would settle the question?

For each scheme, residents need the current decision notice, executed Section 106 agreement, condition-discharge records, affordable tenure schedule and occupation triggers. Infrastructure evidence should cover cumulative traffic, schools including SEND, NHS primary care, drainage and sewer capacity, utilities, public transport, biodiversity and maintenance. A payment or reserved school plot is not the same as an operational service.

Why there is no grand total for these articles

Several entries overlap: Northstone is within South Heywood; Foundry Fields implements the Roch Valley allocation; Barratt’s Stakehill application is within a larger allocation. Lower Falinge replaces existing homes. Completed plots and care-home beds need different treatment. Adding every headline number would produce a misleading total.

Scope and evidence date

Research checked 14 October 2026. This series covers 22 identified major development and regeneration topics across Rochdale borough. It is not a census of every small planning application. Some developments already have occupied homes; asking prices are snapshots. The articles will be updated when outstanding information becomes available.

Secured money, receipts and spending are different

The council’s 2024/25 Infrastructure Funding Statement records £1,522,730 secured through new agreements and £1,629,989 received from agreements across the borough. Of education receipts that year, £619,533 was allocated and none yet spent; separately, £417,976 of older education contributions was spent. It would be false to say no education money was spent. The summary does not identify each development’s payments, school places or occupation triggers. It lists new agreements for Hawks View and Silver Hill, but cannot replace their full signed deeds.

The school forecast is an assessment, not an opening guarantee

The December 2025 primary-school report forecasts Heywood Reception surpluses of 34 in 2026/27, 61 in 2027/28, 29 in 2028/29 and five in 2029/30, with South Heywood housing and school timing to be monitored. For Middleton it forecasts 28 extra places needed in 2026/27, then surpluses of 40, 71 and nine. It discusses additional classes, including use of an existing Hollins classroom; this review does not establish a development-specific approved capital budget or new-school opening from those forecasts. Forecasts are dated planning estimates, not live admissions availability or proof of spare secondary/SEND capacity.

Pennines capacity and the healthcare warning

The school-plan appendix reports, at its assessment date, 75 spare Reception places in North Pennines and 25 in South Pennines, plus 303 spare Key Stage 1 places. Those area figures cannot be treated as guaranteed capacity beside every new estate. For Simister/Bowlee, the NHS’s September 2026 response identifies existing constraints at nearby practices and ongoing assessments, without publishing a funded expansion timetable. Infrastructure support therefore requires more than the existence of nearby schools, surgeries or stations.

Further information and updates

Some final planning agreements, exact rents and prices, affordable-housing breakdowns and infrastructure funding details are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. The relevant articles will be updated when the information becomes available.

articles.excerpt: Simister and Bowlee’s housing programme crosses the borough boundary. Bury Council identifies 1,550 homes overall, of which 200 would be in Rochdale. Only the Rochdale share belongs in a total of this borough’s new housing.
articles.content_html:
Simister and Bowlee’s housing programme crosses the borough boundary. Bury Council identifies 1,550 homes overall, of which 200 would be in Rochdale. Only the Rochdale share belongs in a total of this borough’s new housing.

The development framework includes a new primary school in the Bury portion, a local centre, a spine road, off-site highway works, active-travel routes, green infrastructure and drainage measures. These are requirements and ambitions for a future neighbourhood, rather than proof that all funding and construction contracts are in place.

Bury’s website cites its own affordable policy rate and an approximate affordable total for the Bury homes. That percentage should not be automatically applied to the Rochdale share. The eventual cross-boundary applications need clear tenure schedules and allocation arrangements.

Residents campaigning against the development raise traffic and drainage concerns. Those are attributed concerns, not verified findings that infrastructure cannot accommodate the plan. The published assessments and conditions must show how risks are addressed.

A specific Rochdale housebuilder and site-specific adverse legal finding have not been verified here. The employment-led Northern Gateway and residential Simister/Bowlee programme should also be kept distinct when explaining approvals.

The core accountability question is whether cross-border delivery provides the services residents actually use, with an enforceable timetable rather than separate promises by different authorities.

Location: Bowlee / Middleton and neighbouring Simister in Bury

Planning stage: Strategic allocation; June 2026 development framework guides later applications

Homes: 1,550 across both boroughs; 200 in Rochdale and 1,350 in Bury

Let or for sale: Affordable housing required; Rochdale-specific number and tenure not established

Land: Largely agricultural land in a former Green Belt allocation

Final planning agreement: Framework/allocation evidence: no executed cross-border development agreement for a detailed housing scheme established.

Exact rents / prices: No exact future rent, sale price, service charge or estate-charge schedule was established from the council/government material reviewed; no reliable scheme-specific current quotation was identified.

Affordable breakdown: 200 of the 1,550 homes are in Rochdale. The Bury affordable percentage must not be applied automatically to those 200; Rochdale-specific signed tenure counts are not established.

Funded school capacity: The framework includes a primary school in Bury. No construction budget, funding agreement, opening date or guaranteed Rochdale pupil access established in the reviewed framework.

Funded healthcare capacity: NHS Greater Manchester’s 1 September 2026 response says it is working with five of six nearby GP practices on estates solutions for existing capacity constraints. NHS Property Services is undertaking capacity assessments. The response provides no funded expansion budget, extra appointment/staffing figures or delivery date.

Funded transport capacity: A spine road, off-site works and active-travel routes are planned. No executed scheme-wide funding/delivery schedule or funded increase in bus capacity established.

The published material reviewed does not establish the total number of secured affordable homes or their rents. Individual phases must therefore be assessed separately. Northstone’s homes are already within the 1,000-home masterplan and cannot be added again.

Trub Farm is intended to deliver 158 affordable homes through MCI Developments and Legal & General Affordable Homes. Reported plans comprise 48 apartments and 110 houses, with homes for social rent and shared ownership.

The distinction between these tenures is crucial. Social rent is a rental product; shared ownership involves buying a share and meeting additional ongoing costs. Until the final schedule is available, the total should not be described as 158 social-rented homes.

The reporting contains a date discrepancy. An August 2025 article records a committee vote in favour, subject to a legal agreement, while an August 2026 deal article describes approval the previous month. The decision notice and agreement are needed to reconcile a committee resolution with formal permission.

The council committee report identifies open grassland within the urban boundary, adjoining Green Belt rather than simply being described as a Green Belt farm. Its consultation responses require mitigation, but do not establish an already funded expansion in school or GP capacity.

The regulator’s 2026 casework review records strong inspection grades for L&G Affordable Homes and oversight of third-party repairs providers. That provides relevant landlord context, rather than a promise about homes not yet occupied. If delivered, Trub Farm would directly expand affordable options, but exact rents, shares and service charges remain essential missing information.

articles.excerpt: Rochdale Daily is celebrating 86,000 readers in the last 30 days, thanking the borough for its support and setting an ambitious goal of reaching 200,000 readers by November.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Daily has reached an incredible milestone: 86,000 readers over the past 30 days. To every person who has opened one of our articles, shared a story, sent us an email or helped us reach a neighbour — thank you.

We are humbled. We are grateful. And, most of all, we are delighted that so many people across our borough have chosen to make Rochdale Daily part of their day.

We built this independent newspaper around a simple belief: Rochdale deserves local news that is open, accessible and free from party-political allegiance. We want to bring you unfiltered reporting — stories that celebrate our communities, champion our businesses, ask difficult questions and hold public institutions to account without telling readers what they should think.

Eighty-six thousand readers in a month means something to us because behind every number is a person: a parent checking what is happening at school, a resident following a council decision, a family looking for something to do, a small business hoping to be noticed or a neighbour who simply wants to understand the place they call home.

We want you to know that we read every email. We value your tips, your corrections, your concerns and your encouragement. Some of the stories that matter most begin when one resident takes the time to get in touch.

And we have a big ambition for what comes next: to reach 200,000 readers by November. It is an ambitious target, not a forecast, but we want more people across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough, Milnrow and the wider borough to know that their local stories have a home here.

If you have enjoyed an article, please leave a comment. If you disagree, tell us why. If something important is happening in your street or community, get in touch. Follow the Rochdale Daily Facebook page and share our articles with friends, family and neighbours.

Your comments, questions and suggestions help shape what we investigate and where we direct our attention. We won't always get everything right, and when we don't, we want to hear about it, correct mistakes and do better.

We do not want this to be a newspaper that talks at Rochdale. We want it to be a newspaper that listens to Rochdale.

To all 86,000 of you: thank you for putting your trust in us. We intend to work to earn it every day.

Please comment, follow, share and stay with us. This is your newspaper. We want to work for you — and for our town.

With heartfelt thanks, the Rochdale Daily team.

articles.title: 21 YEARS IN ENGLAND'S BOTTOM 100: Central Rochdale neighbourhood ranked 24th most deprived
articles.excerpt: Government figures show a part of Central Rochdale ranked among England's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods in every index since 2004. Where did regeneration funding go — and what can actually be proved about residents' outcomes?
articles.content_html:
ROCHDALE DAILY INVESTIGATION | 12 OCTOBER 2026

A small part of central Rochdale has been ranked among England's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods in every national assessment since 2004. In the latest official figures it is 24th out of 33,755 areas — and one of just three places in England to have remained in that bottom 100 across all six releases over 21 years.

The finding is not an opposition-party accusation or a campaign slogan. It appears in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government's English Indices of Deprivation 2025. Its code is E01005482, its statistical name Rochdale 010C, and it falls within the wider Central Rochdale and Mandale Park area.

Official sources: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, English Indices of Deprivation 2025 statistical release https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release; Government neighbourhood explorer https://deprivation.communities.gov.uk/about-your-neighbourhood/E01005482; Government research report https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-research-report

2004. 2007. 2010. 2015. 2019. 2025.

The government's researchers identified only three neighbourhoods that were among the 100 most deprived in every one of those six releases: Rochdale 010C, Middlesbrough 003F and Wirral 011C. The government's research report places the Rochdale neighbourhood within the middle-layer area known as Central Rochdale and Mandale Park.

This is not a description of the whole borough and not even of all Central Rochdale. A Lower-layer Super Output Area is a small census-based statistical area, typically home to around 1,500–1,600 people. The boundary of the LSOA matters when discussing local projects and spending. The Department for Education, for example, locates Whitehall Academy on Whitehall Street inside Rochdale 010C, confirming part of the geography, but the area cannot be equated simply with all of Mandale Park or Rochdale town centre.

Source: Department for Education establishment record for Whitehall Academy, LSOA Rochdale 010C https://get-information-schools.service.gov.uk/Establishments/Establishment/Details/151391

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRIVING THE RANKING?

The 2025 government neighbourhood explorer states that employment deprivation is among the area's most severe problems: fewer than 1% of English neighbourhoods rank as more employment deprived. Rochdale 010C also ranks as the most deprived neighbourhood within the borough for income, with higher-than-usual income deprivation affecting children and older people.

The national index measures seven different types of deprivation: income, employment, education, health, crime, barriers to housing and services, and the living environment. Income and employment carry the largest weights at 22.5% each. In other words, the central issue here is not whether a street looks attractive after regeneration; it is the resources and opportunities available to the people who live there.

Source: Government deprivation explorer https://deprivation.communities.gov.uk/about-your-neighbourhood/E01005482; methodology and domain weights https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release

DOES THIS PROVE THAT ROCHDALE HAS BECOME POORER?

No. The government explicitly warns that deprivation rankings describe RELATIVE circumstances. They do not, on their own, measure absolute changes in poverty, wages, health or household income. Boundaries and methods have changed; the 2025 index includes 55 indicators rather than 39 in 2019. Residents could have experienced improvements while their area's national relative position remained extremely poor.

But staying among the 100 most deprived on six separate occasions is nonetheless compelling evidence of persistent relative disadvantage. A serious assessment of whether interventions worked requires more than a new building or investment headline: longitudinal data on earnings, employment, child poverty, housing quality, health and skills, combined with a clear account of which projects actually reached Rochdale 010C.

Source: Government statistical release and guidance https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release

THE REGENERATION MONEY: BIG HEADLINES, BUT WHICH STREETS?

In a 2023 article, Labour council leader Neil Emmott described a £400 million Rochdale town-centre investment programme, including projects such as Riverside, Upperbanks and the restored Town Hall. The council also says the town secured £23.6 million from the government's Towns Fund, intended to support regeneration, skills and connectivity over a wider geographic area. These are genuine funding and development announcements.

Yet neither £400 million nor £23.6 million is an audited total spent exclusively within Rochdale 010C. The figures include a range of projects, investment types, funding sources and locations. Treating either sum as money spent on the approximately 1,600 residents of this one neighbourhood would be misleading.

Sources: Rochdale Council leader's 2023 regeneration statement https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-leaders-blog/investing-future-boroughs-regeneration-continues; council Towns Fund overview https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/business-licensing/towns-fund-money-help-us-improve-rochdale

One more closely relevant entry does appear in Rochdale's formal capital programme: the 2025/26 budget shows £450,000 in external grant funding scheduled for 'Towns Fund – New Homes Central Rochdale', described as land acquisition and remediation before homes are built by Rochdale Boroughwide Housing and private developers. An earlier programme showed £360,000 scheduled in 2023/24 for the similarly named project.

But these are BUDGET entries, not proof that either amount was actually spent. 'Central Rochdale' is also a broader project designation than LSOA Rochdale 010C. The missing link is a project-by-project ledger with actual expenditure, precise sites, housing completions and beneficiary outcomes.

Sources: Rochdale capital programme 2025/26 to 2029/30, 'Towns Fund – New Homes Central Rochdale' https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s112547/Append.%201%20for%20Capital%20Programme%20202526%20to%20202930.pdf; 2023/24 capital programme https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s94502/Append.%205%20for%20Budget%20Report%20202324.pdf

WHAT HAS BEEN DONE ABOUT POVERTY?

The council approved 'The Future We Deserve', its borough-wide 2024–2029 anti-poverty strategy, in March 2024. The authority described rising destitution and inequality as reasons for taking a long-term approach. From April 2026 it also began allocating around £5 million in government-backed Crisis and Resilience Fund support across the borough to assist residents facing emergencies, housing pressures and the cost of essentials.

Those programmes matter. They are also different in purpose from capital investment: emergency food and housing support can reduce immediate hardship, while regeneration may seek longer-term jobs and productivity. Neither a borough-wide budget nor a policy document establishes how many residents of Rochdale 010C received support or whether the area's underlying deprivation indicators improved.

Sources: March 2024 Cabinet decision approving anti-poverty strategy https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieIssueDetails.aspx?IId=55806&Opt=3; council Crisis and Resilience Fund https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/cost-living/crisis-resilience-fund

THE COUNCIL'S OWN RESPONSE TO SOCIAL MOBILITY CONCERNS

In a 2025 response to a social-mobility investigation, Rochdale Council acknowledged significant poverty, deprivation and inequality while pointing to improvements in town centres, education, employment opportunities and transport. It highlighted Rochdale Sixth Form College, Hopwood Hall College, the restored Town Hall and wider development proposals as assets that could improve opportunity.

These represent reasonable arguments for regeneration. But they are evidence of provision and investment, not by themselves proof that low-income residents in Rochdale 010C have entered stable, well-paid work or escaped hardship. This investigation has not obtained an LSOA-specific outcomes evaluation to test that claim.

WHO SHOULD ANSWER?

Rochdale Council is Labour-controlled, led by Councillor Neil Emmott. The Central Rochdale ward is represented in October 2026 by Councillor Farooq Ahmed (Workers Party of Britain), Councillor Waqar Khan (Workers Party of Britain) and Councillor Sameena Zaheer (Labour and Co-operative), who also holds a Cabinet portfolio for Corporate, Governance and Transformation. The ward is a different boundary from the statistical neighbourhood and its current councillors did not all serve throughout the 21-year period.

These affiliations identify democratic responsibility and representation; the deprivation index does not establish misconduct, negligence or causation by any individual councillor or political party.

SEVEN QUESTIONS THAT DESERVE DOCUMENTED ANSWERS

1. Which completed, current and planned projects since 2004 have physically overlapped the boundary of LSOA E01005482?

2. For each project, how much public funding was approved, contracted and actually spent — separated from private investment and borough-wide allocations?

3. What proportion of jobs created or safeguarded under those programmes went to residents of this exact neighbourhood, and at what wages?

4. How have child income deprivation, employment deprivation, housing conditions and school attendance changed in absolute terms over time, not merely national rankings?

5. What specific measurable targets did the 2024–2029 Anti-Poverty Strategy set for the most deprived neighbourhoods, and how does Rochdale 010C perform against them?

6. What data will the council use to demonstrate that forthcoming developments are benefiting the people already living in this neighbourhood, rather than simply changing the appearance or population mix of nearby streets?

7. Will the council publish an independently auditable, geographically itemised account of 20 years of spending and outcomes, and allow residents to examine the results?

WHY IT MATTERS

Rochdale's new shops, college provision, housing developments, town-hall restoration and cultural attractions are visible and can produce genuine benefits. The government's latest deprivation statistics show a different and equally important side of local economic life: one neighbourhood has remained among England's most deprived in every national index for more than two decades.

That is not proof that £400 million was wasted. It is proof that the success of regeneration cannot be established from the value of construction projects alone. The ultimate test is whether residents gain lasting opportunities, better homes, improved health and higher disposable incomes.

articles.title: Rochdale Council to implement new planning decision rules from October 31
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council will shift more planning applications to officers under new rules effective from October 31, aiming to streamline decision-making and focus committees on larger proposals.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council is set to implement revised planning decision procedures starting October 31, 2026. The new rules will see a significant shift in how planning applications are processed, with more decisions being made by planning officers rather than elected committees. This change follows the Government's guidance under the Town and Country Planning (Discharge of Local Planning Authority Functions) (England) Regulations 2026.

Under the new system, applications will be categorised into two schedules. Schedule One will include householder applications, minor commercial and residential proposals, lawful development certificates, and technical matters, all of which must be determined by planning officers. Schedule Two will encompass larger developments, listed building consents, advertisement consents, tree preservation orders, and legal agreements with developers, which can be referred to the planning committee but require agreement between a nominated councillor and a nominated officer.

The council's report indicates that the Government aims to provide greater clarity regarding the role of planning committees, allowing them to focus on significant proposals while routine decisions are handled by officers. Councillors will still be able to engage with planning matters, raise residents' concerns, and submit material planning reasons, but a councillor's request alone will not necessitate committee consideration. Additionally, the previous threshold for the number of objections required to trigger committee review will no longer apply.

The council has warned that decisions made by planning committees on applications that should be handled by officers could face legal challenges, potentially leading to judicial reviews. As the new rules come into effect, residents and stakeholders in Rochdale will need to be aware of these changes and their implications for local planning processes.

articles.title: High Court rules against filmmaker in Hopwood Hall restoration dispute
articles.excerpt: A recent High Court ruling has concluded a legal battle between American filmmaker Hopwood DePree and Rochdale Council over the future of Hopwood Hall in Middleton.
articles.content_html:
A High Court ruling has determined that American filmmaker Hopwood DePree does not have the right to purchase Hopwood Hall, a Grade-II* listed building in Middleton, following a protracted legal dispute with Rochdale Council. The decision was announced during a hearing at the Manchester Civil Justice Centre last week, marking a significant setback for DePree, who has invested over £750,000 in efforts to restore the historic estate.

The saga began in 2017 when DePree signed an options agreement with the council to lead the redevelopment of Hopwood Hall. His vision included transforming the 1400s stately home into a wedding and hospitality venue, complete with a hotel retreat, gift shop, and guided tours. DePree engaged the local community in his restoration efforts, which included extensive work on the hall's gardens and interior.

Before DePree's involvement, Hopwood Hall had fallen into disrepair, with its last known use being as part of De La Salle College, which closed in 1989. The hall had previously served as a venue for various events, including an underground bar and nightclub during the 1960s and 70s, where notable acts such as Black Sabbath performed.

The ruling concludes a decade-long effort by DePree to revive the hall, which has been under the ownership of Rochdale Council since the college's closure. The future of Hopwood Hall now remains uncertain as the council considers its next steps regarding the estate.
