evidence_sources.captured_text: The Hopwood Hall saga | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The Hopwood Hall saga George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 10, 2026 | 8:44 AM Print The Grade-II listed Hopwood Hall in Middleton When an American filmmaker and Rochdale council signed an agreement over a shared ambition to restore Hopwood Hall, no one could have fathomed the furious saga that unfolded. What started as a harmonious relationship between Hopwood DePree and the local authority ended up with them being on opposite sides of a court room. Mr DePree claims ancestral connections to the Grade-II* listed building in Middleton. His dream was to bring the 1400s stately home back to life. He even roped in the local community to help him do it, apparently spending more than £750,000 on the project. On what he described as a ‘sad day’ in Manchester Civil Justice Centre last week, his dream was crushed. The High Court ruled in favour of the council following a legal battle over whether Mr DePree had the right to buy the estate or not. The saga began in 2017 when Hopwood DePree signed an options agreement with town hall bosses to lead the redevelopment of the hall. Since then he has led a decade-long community effort to do exactly that. The Hollywood man’s vision saw the hall transformed into a wedding and hospitality venue, with a hotel ‘retreat’, gift shop and guided tours all part of the package. His team could regularly be seen working on the hall’s gardens and titivating the interior in the years since. Before Mr DePree came along, the hall had fallen into disrepair and irrelevance. Its last known use was as part of the De La Salle College, which shut down in 1989. During the 1960s and 70s it was said to be the setting for an underground bar and nightclub. It is believed that Ozzy Osbourne’s band Black Sabbath and other iconic performers played there. Since the closure of the college, the hall has been in the possession of Rochdale council. The American even created a Youtube series and wrote a book about his journey refurbishing what he affectionately called ‘Downton Shabby’. However, this journey came to an abrupt halt when the council ended the agreement in October 2024 and, without warning, barred Mr DePree and his group from the building. Part of the options agreement allowed the US actor and producer to purchase the historic asset from landowners Rochdale council for a ‘peppercorn fee’ – £1. Mr DePree attempted to exercise that option the day before the council ended the agreement, which was denied by town hall chiefs. Since then, a two-year-long war of words has raged between Mr DePree and Rochdale council. The American threatened legal action for months, but the council never budged. Mr DePree believed the local authority acted unlawfully by denying his ‘legally binding’ option to buy Hopwood Hall. At the time, the council said they ended the agreement because Mr DePree hadn’t made enough progress with the restoration effort. This expulsion from the estate came following a number of extensions to the agreement made by the council. The local authority even granted ‘change of use’ planning permission to Mr DePree for Hopwood Hall in 2022. Until the two sides decided to settle the matter in High Court, it was unclear just how important that planning permission was. Effectively, approved planning permission was the trigger to open up the option for Mr DePree to have the estate transferred to him. The High Court played host to Hopwood Hall Estate Ltd vs Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council this week. In the words of Mr DePree’s barrister, Ashley Bowes, the planning permission was ‘the star of the show’. The court heard details of the dispute over whether Mr DePree had authority to trigger the transfer of the property based on the approved plans. The council’s barrister Geraint Wheatley said the plans did not go far enough in demonstrating a serious commitment to reinstate and refurbish the 1400s building, as required by the options agreement. He described the ‘ruined’ hall as needing far more than some internal works to bring it back to a state of habitation. According to Mr Wheatley the conditions of the options agreement to trigger the purchase of the hall had four elements – authorisation to reinstate and refurbish the building; agreed standard of refurbishment between the parties (fit for habitation); English Heritage approval; and that the property would be reinstated and refurbished in whole, not in part. The defence barrister pointed out that getting permission for events and hospitality space for part of the ground floor doesn’t relate to the building ‘in whole’, as requested in the agreement clause. He also pointed out that the plans wouldn’t have seen the hall be fit for habitation or reinstated and refurbished. “Obtaining a mere ‘change of use’ permission doesn’t show a great deal of commitment,” Mr Wheatley told the court. “Plans of physical work show that commitment.” Mr Wheatley also tried to argue that English Heritage approval wasn’t given. But His Honour Judge Hodge KC believed the organisation’s support for the 2022 plans qualified as their approval. Buoyed by the judge agreeing with one point of the claimant, Dr Bowes said the 2022 application was internal work that would have created an events and hospitality space and enabled future work to be reinstated and refurbished. He said the claimant didn’t think anything more than a change of use application would be necessary to trigger the purchase as it wasn’t specified in the agreement. Dr Bowes said it was ‘wishful thinking’ on the council’s part that a community group would spend huge sums of money drawing up plans for physical works when they didn’t think it would be necessary. After delving into detailed planning legislation; the interpretation of wording in the agreement; and the cross-examinations of both Hopwood DePree and council boss for economy and place, Mark Robinson, the judge ruled in favour of the defendant – Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council. His Honour Judge Hodge KC described how the planning application did not cover the whole of the property or showcase the ability to reinstate and refurbish Hopwood Hall, as required in the options agreement. He added: “I am satisfied, for the reasons I have given, that the planning permission does not satisfy the requirements of the options agreement. I therefore refuse to grant the relief sought by the claimant.” A lengthy saga was ended by a two-day trial. Instead of getting Hopwood Hall for £1, Mr DePree was landed with a £114,000 bill to cover the council’s court costs. However, the American said the fight isn’t over and Hopwood Hall ‘must be saved’. He didn’t confirm whether his team would appeal the judgement, but they have until November 18 to do so. Speaking after the case, Mr DePree said: “Obviously I am incredibly disappointed. Not just me but the community of support around the world and the UK charitable groups as well. “I am already discussing with my legal team about the next steps. In the meantime I hope Rochdale council will be watching over Hopwood Hall because we will be keeping an eye on them. “We are not giving up. Hopwood Hall must be saved. In the two years we have been locked out the gardens have gone into wrack and ruin. I hope they will step up and save the hall. I still think the community group and I are the best people to take this forward. “I am getting messages from around the world with people offering money and support. It is a sad day but we will have to have a look at our options.” The town hall has committed to maintaining the building and have commissioned a feasibility study to look into possible future uses for the historic asset. A Rochdale council spokesperson said: “We are pleased with today’s judgement. It’s a shame that we had to endure a costly court battle to get to this point, as the time and money invested into this process could have been better spent on the hall itself. “We’re now focussed on moving forward. More than £1.6m has been spent on the hall by ourselves and Historic England since 2017 and we will continue to invest in vital repairs to this historic building. Feasibility studies have already been completed and options for Hopwood Hall’s long-term future will be considered in due course. “One thing we are clear on is, whatever the future holds for Hopwood Hall, this building, once restored and refurbished, will be used for the benefit of the wider community of Middleton who rightly cherish it as an important part of Middleton’s rich and varied heritage.” Add Roch Valley Radio as a preferred source on Google News to see more of our local reporting Add as a preferred source on Google Do you have a story for us? articles.title: Rochdale's music heritage celebrated in New album 'Kenion Street'
articles.excerpt: The album 'Kenion Street', believed to be the first commercial release by a UK council, showcases local talent and pays tribute to the town's rich musical history.
articles.content_html:
An album titled 'Kenion Street', believed to be the first commercial release by a UK council, has gained significant attention, reaching millions of listeners on national radio and streaming platforms. Launched as part of Rochdale's year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture, the album features local artists performing reimagined versions of classic tracks recorded at the town's iconic studios.

From 1977 to 2001, Rochdale was home to Suite Sixteen and Cargo Studios, located on Kenion Street, where renowned artists such as OMD, The Stone Roses, Happy Mondays, Joy Division, and Inspiral Carpets recorded some of their most memorable work. The album includes 11 tracks, featuring PoolEra's rendition of OMD's 'Electricity', Medley's version of New Order's 'Dreams Never End', and Jennifer Read's interpretation of The Fall's 'Totally Wired'.

All tracks were recorded and produced at Voltalab Sound Studios, situated in the original Cargo/Suite Sixteen building, by studio founder Jamie Alsop. The album has received positive reviews and was featured on Radio 6 Music, where Middleton band K-Estate's cover of Gang of Four's 'Damaged Goods' was highlighted as Track of the Day. Other tracks have been played across various stations, including XS Manchester and Mersey Radio, reaching a combined audience of over 3.5 million.

The release of 'Kenion Street' not only showcases local talent but also serves as a reminder of Rochdale's significant contribution to the music industry. The album's success may inspire further initiatives to celebrate and promote the town's rich musical heritage.

It was also made Track of the Day on Radio X with other tracks played across XS Manchester, Mersey Radio, Phoenix FM and many more, with a combined audience of over 3.5 million. articles.title: Sara Rowbotham: the Rochdale health worker who raised 181 safeguarding alerts
articles.excerpt: Sara Rowbotham repeatedly raised concerns about vulnerable young people while working for Rochdale’s Crisis Intervention Team, later giving evidence to Parliament about the response to child sexual exploitation in the town.
articles.content_html:
Sara Rowbotham became one of the most recognisable figures associated with the response to child sexual exploitation in Rochdale after repeatedly raising concerns about vulnerable young people while working for the town’s NHS Crisis Intervention Team.

Rowbotham worked as the Crisis Intervention Team Co-ordinator and Sexual Health Improvement Specialist. The team was established in 2004 and supported thousands of young people, including those who disclosed concerns about sexual abuse and exploitation.

In evidence to the House of Commons Home Affairs Committee in November 2012, Rowbotham told MPs that, over a period covering the years from 2005 to 2011, her team had identified referrals involving 103 young people.

She also told the committee that she had made 181 alerts to Children’s Social Care about concerns involving young people.

Asked whether she believed police and social services had worked together effectively, Rowbotham said this had happened “very rarely” in the early period and that she had subsequently begun making the Safeguarding Children Unit aware of the referrals so that strategy meetings could be convened.

The committee also heard evidence from other senior officials about the handling of the information. The subsequent Home Affairs Committee report described missed opportunities and examined the response of children's social care and police to child sexual exploitation in Rochdale.

Rowbotham told MPs that she had repeatedly tried to make protective services aware of the vulnerability of young people and that she believed agencies had failed to provide a sufficiently comprehensive and coordinated response.

The evidence came after the prosecution of nine men in Rochdale in 2012 for serious sexual offences against girls. The case prompted wider scrutiny of how authorities had responded to reports of child sexual exploitation.

Rowbotham continued to speak publicly about the response. In 2014, she was made redundant from her role. Contemporary reporting by ITV News and The Guardian documented her concerns about the handling of the case and the impact of losing her position.

Her story later reached a much wider audience when the BBC drama Three Girls was broadcast in May 2017, with Maxine Peake portraying Rowbotham.

A petition calling for Rowbotham to be formally recognised attracted more than 100,000 signatures within days of the programme airing and ultimately exceeded 275,000 signatures, according to contemporary reports.

Rowbotham subsequently entered local politics. She was elected as a councillor for North Middleton in 2015 and went on to serve as Deputy Leader of Rochdale Borough Council and as a cabinet member.

Her public recognition also continued. She received a Special Recognition Award at the NHS Heroes Awards in 2018 and was made an honorary member of the NSPCC Council that year. In 2021, she was appointed MBE for services to young people.

Rowbotham’s evidence to Parliament remains part of the official record of the scrutiny that followed the Rochdale child sexual exploitation cases. Her account of the 181 alerts, and questions about how information held by frontline services was acted upon, formed part of the wider examination of safeguarding failures in the town.

Source: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee evidence and report; contemporary reporting by ITV News and The Guardian; Rochdale Borough Council records.

articles.title: New Awaab’s Law protections could cover millions more renters and vulnerable households
articles.excerpt: A government consultation will examine extending Awaab’s Law to private renters and other accommodation, with faster legal deadlines for landlords to tackle serious hazards such as damp and mould.
articles.content_html:
Millions more households could receive stronger legal protections against dangerous housing conditions under plans to extend Awaab’s Law beyond social housing.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government has launched a consultation on how the law could be introduced for private renters and whether similar protections should apply to other forms of accommodation.

Awaab’s Law currently provides legal deadlines for social landlords to investigate and address serious hazards, including dangerous damp and mould. The measures were introduced in memory of two-year-old Awaab Ishak, who died in 2020 after prolonged exposure to damp and mould in his home.

The proposed extension could mean around nine million households are covered by new repair timescales, compared with around four million currently covered.

The consultation is considering protections for private rented homes as well as:

temporary accommodation for homeless people and families;

accommodation for young people leaving care; and

supported housing, including accommodation used by older, disabled and other vulnerable people.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook said all renters should be able to expect a safe and decent home, regardless of tenure.

“Awaab’s Law is already helping to drive up standards in the social housing sector. We’re now moving to extend it to private landlords so that England’s 11 million private renters can enjoy the same protections,” he said.

The government says landlords are already required to act when serious hazards are identified. Around one in 10 private rented homes is estimated to contain a Category 1 hazard, the most serious level.

The Renters’ Rights Act has also introduced fines of up to £7,000 where serious dangers are found. Awaab’s Law would add legally defined timescales requiring action on the most serious conditions.

The consultation will help determine how Awaab’s Law should operate in the private rented sector, including the timescales for the new protections to come into force. It closes on 18 December 2026.

Generation Rent welcomed the move. Chief Executive Holly Williamson said too many renters live in homes that can harm their health and wait months for landlords to address problems.

Crisis also backed the proposals, highlighting the conditions faced by people living in temporary accommodation, including hostels and bed and breakfasts.

The Renters’ Reform Coalition said nobody should have to live in a home that makes them ill or puts their life at risk, while Independent Age said older renters can face serious problems including rats and mould and may be afraid to request repairs.

Independent Age said almost 96% of older renters it polled supported Awaab’s Law.

Become, the national charity for children in care and young care leavers, also welcomed the government’s consideration of stronger standards for accommodation used by young people leaving care.

The proposals form part of commitments in the Renters’ Rights Act and the National Plan to End Homelessness.

The government says the changes are intended to ensure dangerous housing conditions are dealt with quickly and that tenants can raise concerns without fear of repercussions.

Source: Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government.

articles.title: Inside abandoned Simpson Clough Paper Mill — and why urban exploration carries serious risks
articles.excerpt: A YouTube video has taken viewers inside the abandoned Simpson Clough Paper Mill near Rochdale, revealing remnants of its industrial past while highlighting the fascination — and dangers — of urban exploration.
articles.content_html:
An abandoned paper mill near Rochdale where machinery, equipment and remnants of its working life appear to have been left behind has been documented by urban explorers.

Footage titled 'We Found The ABANDONED Simpson Clough Paper Mill Hidden In Rochdale With Everything Left Behind!' takes viewers inside Simpson Clough Mill, offering a glimpse into an industrial site normally hidden from public view.

Watch the exploration: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pCnxD574cB8

The mill has a long industrial history. Local historical records describe Simpson Clough Mills as beginning as a fulling mill in the 1840s before being purchased by Cromptons in 1939, used for food storage during the Second World War and converted to paper manufacture after the war. The site later operated as Union Papertech and closed in January 2023.

The footage captures much of what has made so-called urban exploration, or urbex, enormously popular online. Instead of seeing industrial history restored and labelled inside a museum, viewers see workplaces in their abandoned state: machinery, offices, workshops and the gradual effects of time and nature.

For a borough whose identity was profoundly shaped by mills, manufacturing and the Industrial Revolution, sites such as Simpson Clough have an obvious historical fascination. They can provide a visual record of workplaces where generations of people spent their working lives.

But urban exploration has another side which should not be overlooked. Abandoned industrial buildings can be extremely dangerous. Water penetration, corrosion, structural deterioration and years without routine maintenance can leave floors, roofs and staircases unsafe. Broken glass, exposed metal, electrical hazards, contaminated water and hazardous materials can create further risks.

Someone injured deep inside a large former industrial complex may also be difficult for emergency services to locate and rescue.

The legal position is more complicated than saying that entering every abandoned building automatically amounts to a criminal offence. Ordinary trespass in England and Wales is generally a civil matter, but abandoned buildings and the land surrounding them still have owners. Entering private property without permission can amount to trespass, while damaging fences, doors or windows, taking property, or entering certain protected sites can raise separate criminal issues.

Rochdale Daily does not know whether the people responsible for the Simpson Clough footage had permission to enter the site and makes no allegation that any offence was committed.

The fascination with urbex is nevertheless understandable. There is something extraordinary about seeing a workplace after the workers have gone. Desks, machinery and ordinary objects can become accidental historical artefacts, and videos produced by explorers have created an informal online record of parts of Britain's disappearing industrial landscape.

The challenge is preserving that history without people putting themselves in danger or entering places unlawfully. Property owners can grant controlled access to photographers, historians and filmmakers, while heritage organisations can document industrial buildings before redevelopment or demolition.

That could be particularly valuable around Rochdale, Heywood and the surrounding valleys, where surviving industrial sites tell an important part of the borough's story.

Simpson Clough is another reminder that extraordinary pieces of local industrial history can sit quietly behind walls and fences long after their original purpose has disappeared. They are fascinating to see — but no photograph or video is worth serious injury to obtain.

Rochdale Daily does not encourage entry onto private, abandoned or restricted property without permission. Anyone wishing to document a disused site should seek the landowner's permission and follow appropriate safety requirements.

articles.title: Norden residents report being without water since Friday morning as outage continues
articles.excerpt: Residents in Norden say they have been without water since around 9am on Friday, with households reporting an extended loss of supply and frustration over the apparent lack of an on-site response.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Norden are reporting that they have been without running water since around 9am on Friday, with the disruption continuing into Saturday and households asking when their supply will return.

Rochdale Daily has received reports from residents describing a prolonged loss of supply and saying they have seen no sign of United Utilities teams in their immediate area. At the time of publication, Rochdale Daily has not independently confirmed the cause, the precise number of properties affected or an estimated restoration time.

The length of the reported interruption is significant. United Utilities' published standards say that where a burst on one of its pipes causes an unexpected loss of supply, it aims to restore water within 12 hours. The company says that where it identifies that it has failed to restore supply within 12 hours, household customers should automatically receive £50, plus another £50 for each additional 12-hour period they remain without water. Eligibility will depend on the circumstances of the interruption and the company's standards.

WHAT SHOULD RESIDENTS DO?

Anyone still without water should report the problem directly to United Utilities, even if neighbours have already done so. Its 24-hour water and wastewater number is 0345 672 3723. Residents can also use the United Utilities website to check for active incidents affecting their postcode and report water-supply problems.

If neighbouring properties have water but yours does not, United Utilities advises carrying out basic household checks. The internal stop tap, commonly located beneath the kitchen sink, can be turned off and back on several times while the cold kitchen tap is running, which may clear an airlock or obstruction. If an entire street or neighbourhood is affected, the problem is more likely to be on the wider network and should be reported to the company.

Residents should keep a record of when their supply stopped, any reference numbers given by United Utilities, screenshots of incident updates and details of calls or messages. This may be useful if the interruption later qualifies for a standards-of-service payment or if a complaint needs to be escalated.

VULNERABLE RESIDENTS AND BOTTLED WATER

People who are older, disabled, have medical needs, mobility difficulties, young children at home or otherwise need additional support should tell United Utilities immediately and ask about its free Priority Services scheme.

United Utilities says that if water is likely to remain off for more than 12 hours it will try to make alternative supplies available in the affected area. Priority Services customers who cannot collect alternative supplies may be able to receive bottled water at home.

Priority Services can be contacted on 0345 072 6093. United Utilities' published Priority Services commitments also include bottled-water support during qualifying prolonged emergency interruptions, with enhanced arrangements for its most vulnerable customers.

Residents who rely on water for home dialysis or another essential medical treatment should make this clear when contacting the company rather than waiting for a general area update.

If United Utilities confirms an alternative bottled-water collection point, Rochdale Daily will add the location to this story.

WHAT ABOUT COMPENSATION?

United Utilities' current standards of service state that an unexpected mains interruption lasting beyond 12 hours can trigger an automatic £50 payment, followed by a further £50 for each additional 12-hour period without water where the relevant standard applies. Residents should therefore retain evidence of the duration of the outage and check subsequent bills or correspondence.

If an eligible payment is not made, customers can raise the matter directly with United Utilities through its complaints process.

Rochdale Daily has sought further information on the cause of the Norden disruption, the number of properties affected, what work is under way, whether alternative water supplies are being provided and when residents can expect normal service to return.

This is a developing story and will be updated as further verified information becomes available.

articles.title: £45 for Feel Good Festival? Why today's ticket price has sparked complaints — and what organisers say
articles.excerpt: The £45 on-the-day price for Rochdale Feel Good Festival's main stage has prompted criticism from some residents, but organisers say tickets started at £15 and charging helps reduce reliance on public funding as festival costs rise.
articles.content_html:
A £45 on-the-day ticket price for the main stage at Rochdale Feel Good Festival has prompted criticism from some residents, with questions being raised about affordability in a borough where many households are already feeling the pressure of the cost of living.

One resident summed up the frustration, saying: "Knew it was going to happen ‘it’s for the people of the town’ the same town thats poverty ridden and they put a £45 price on it I hope it’s a flop and they go back to doing it for the people of the town."

It is an understandable criticism when £45 is viewed in isolation. For a couple buying on the day, the headline ticket cost is £90 before the 7.5 per cent booking fee. For a larger family or group, the cost can quickly become substantial. There are also no concessions for the main stage ticket.

But £45 is not what everybody attending the festival has paid — and the pricing structure is important context.

Rochdale Borough Council says tickets were deliberately released in phases, with the cheapest tickets available to people who booked earliest. Early-bird tickets cost £15 plus a 7.5 per cent booking fee. Once those sold out, phase two was £25, phase three £30 and phase four £35. Tickets bought on the day cost £45 plus the booking fee.

In other words, somebody who secured an early-bird ticket paid one third of today's £45 headline price. The council's ticket page explicitly told customers that the earlier they booked, the more they would save. Early-bird and subsequent lower-priced allocations sold out before the festival.

The £15 starting price was not hidden until the last minute. Rochdale Development Agency announced on 30 January that early-bird tickets would go on sale on 6 February for £15, followed by a second phase at £25. Rochdale Creates repeated the early-bird price in its own February announcement.

WHY DOES THE FESTIVAL CHARGE AT ALL?

The council has also published a detailed explanation for charging for the main stage. It says the decision was announced in February 2020 as an attempt to make the festival less reliant on public funding.

According to the council, it has invested well over £1 million in Feel Good Festival since the event began in 2008, while the festival has lost 25 per cent of its public funding since 2017. The council says cuts to public spending have squeezed budgets at the same time as the costs of staging festivals have continued to rise.

Those costs, it says, include increasing artist fees as well as inflation affecting production, labour and infrastructure. Organisers argue that asking festival-goers to contribute towards entry to the main stage creates a balance between reducing the burden on taxpayers and keeping a major summer music event in Rochdale.

The council describes the ticket price as modest for a full day of entertainment and says Feel Good Festival contributes to the local economy while also generating income from sponsors and traders.

That does not mean residents have to agree with the decision. There is a legitimate debate about whether a council-backed festival in a borough containing communities with significant deprivation should prioritise the lowest possible admission price, particularly when an event has long been promoted as something for Rochdale residents.

But there is an equally important distinction between saying Feel Good Festival costs £45 and saying that everyone was asked to pay £45. They were not. The final on-the-day price is the top of a phased structure that began at £15.

WHAT IS STILL FREE?

The charge applies specifically to the main stage area at Rochdale Town Hall Square, the food and drink village and associated wristband-access areas. Most performances in the festival's indoor venues remain free.

The main-stage ticket also includes a reusable Rochdale Creates drinks cup, which organisers say is intended to reduce single-use plastic. Visitors can take the cup home or return it to marked collection points for reuse.

So is £45 too expensive? For some Rochdale families, undoubtedly it will feel that way — particularly for anybody deciding to attend at the last minute. The criticism deserves to be heard.

But the complete picture is that tickets began at £15, rose in clearly advertised phases as allocations sold out, and the council says charging was introduced because public funding has fallen while the cost of staging the festival has risen.

Whether that represents a fair way to protect one of Rochdale's biggest annual events, or whether the final price has moved too far away from the idea of a festival 'for the people of the town', is ultimately a question for residents themselves.

articles.title: RBH warns tenants over cold-calling 'claims farmers' offering compensation for repairs
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing says customers are being cold-called by firms offering 'no win, no fee' solicitors for repair claims - a warning that lands against the backdrop of the Awaab Ishak tragedy and the reforms that followed.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing has warned tenants to be on their guard after a number of customers reported being cold-called by a firm asking about property repairs.

The landlord says the callers offered to provide a solicitor to work on tenants' behalf so they could claim compensation. Firms operating this way - sometimes called claims management companies or "claims farmers" - typically describe themselves as offering "no win, no fee" services.

"Be careful - if something sounds too good to be true, it probably is," RBH said, urging anyone with a concern about their home to talk to the landlord directly so it can be sorted. Repairs can be reported via the MyRBH portal at www.myrbh.org.uk, by calling Freephone 0800 027 7769, or by emailing rbh.repairs@rbh.org.uk. RBH says it aims to get things right first time, and tenants who feel it has fallen short can find details of how to complain at www.rbh.org.uk/feedback.

Why this matters in Rochdale

No warning about housing disrepair in this borough can be read in isolation from what happened to Awaab Ishak.

Awaab was two years old when he died in December 2020. In November 2022, a coroner concluded that his death was caused by prolonged exposure to mould in his family's RBH flat on the Freehold estate - mould his parents had repeatedly reported. The case caused national outrage, cost RBH its chief executive, and led directly to Awaab's Law, which sets legal time limits for social landlords in England to investigate and fix damp, mould and other hazards, with the first phase of those duties coming into force in October 2025.

That history cuts two ways. It explains why RBH is now at pains to encourage tenants to report repairs directly and to demonstrate that reports will be acted on - rebuilding confidence that was badly damaged. And it also explains why claims firms see RBH tenants as a market worth cold-calling: disrepair claims against social landlords have grown sharply across the country, and a landlord with RBH's recent history is an obvious target for firms seeking clients.

Tenants are entitled to seek independent legal advice about genuine disrepair, and nothing prevents them doing so. But consumer bodies have long warned that some claims firms take large cuts of any compensation, sign tenants up to agreements with exit fees, or pursue claims that leave tenants worse off than simply having the repair done. A tenant's first and simplest route remains reporting the problem to the landlord - and, if it is not fixed, escalating through the complaints process and then to the Housing Ombudsman, which is free.

The test for RBH is the one Awaab's case set: whether reports of damp, mould and disrepair are fixed properly and fast, first time. If they are, the cold-callers will find little to farm.

articles.title: Are Facebook Groups Becoming the Gatekeepers of Local News?
articles.excerpt: Large community Facebook groups now play a major role in determining which local stories residents see, raising questions about moderation, access to information and the influence of digital gatekeepers.
articles.content_html:
Recent posts from independent local news publishers have, at times, remained pending approval or failed to appear in large community Facebook groups. The reasons are not always clear and may range from routine moderation and administrative delays to editorial decisions made by group administrators.

Whatever the explanation, the situation raises a wider question about how much influence large local Facebook groups have over the news and viewpoints residents are exposed to.

Many of these groups have memberships larger than the circulation of traditional local newspapers. For thousands of people, they have become the primary place where local news, events and community discussion are discovered. Decisions about which posts are approved can therefore have a significant impact on what information reaches the public.

Independent journalism exists to report what is happening within a community, regardless of whether those stories are politically convenient or uncomfortable. It should not matter whether a story reflects positively or negatively on any political party, campaign group or public body. The role of journalism is to inform readers, not to tell them what to think.

Equally, moderation is an important part of running any online community. Administrators are entitled to remove unlawful material, spam, abuse, hate speech or defamatory content. However, where lawful reporting is prevented from reaching large community audiences, it is reasonable to ask whether local people are receiving a balanced picture of events.

Too often, debate can become centred on labels rather than evidence. Terms such as 'misinformation', 'divisive' or 'harmful' should only be used where they can be supported by facts. If reporting is inaccurate, it should be corrected. If facts are disputed, they should be challenged with evidence. Robust debate is healthier than silent suppression.

Independent local journalism has become increasingly important as traditional local newsrooms have shrunk. Smaller publishers often report stories that might otherwise receive little attention, giving residents access to a broader range of information and perspectives.

Ultimately, Facebook groups have become powerful gatekeepers of local information. That influence brings responsibility. While moderators are free to manage their communities as they see fit, readers should also recognise that what appears in a Facebook feed is not necessarily the full picture of what is happening across Rochdale borough.

A healthy democracy depends on people having access to a range of lawful reporting and being trusted to reach their own conclusions.

It is therefore not unusual for residents to notice the aircraft without an immediate explanation being made available.

articles.title: Editorial: Justice remains unfinished in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: More than a decade after the Rochdale grooming gang scandal shocked Britain, the perpetrators have been jailed, reforms have been introduced and institutions have apologised. Yet for many survivors and residents, questions about accountability, trust and whether justice has truly been delivered remain unanswered.
articles.content_html:
More than a decade has passed since the Rochdale child sexual exploitation scandal exposed one of the gravest safeguarding failures in modern British history. The men responsible have been convicted and imprisoned, but the question that continues to confront Rochdale is whether justice ended with those convictions.

Successive independent inquiries have reached strikingly similar conclusions. Reviews by Parliament, local safeguarding bodies and independent investigators found that vulnerable children were repeatedly failed by institutions responsible for protecting them. Victims were too often viewed as making 'lifestyle choices' rather than recognised as children subjected to coercion, rape, trafficking and organised sexual exploitation. Information was not consistently shared between agencies, warning signs were missed, organised offending was underestimated and opportunities to intervene were repeatedly lost.

The testimony of survivors remains among the most compelling evidence of those failures. Girls described repeatedly reporting abuse only to be disbelieved, dismissed as troublesome teenagers or treated as willing participants in their own exploitation. Children who regularly went missing were returned to the same environments where offenders continued to target them. Independent reviews concluded that professionals frequently focused on victims' behaviour rather than the methods of coercion used by organised offenders.

The criminal justice system eventually delivered significant convictions. Operation Span resulted in nine men being convicted in 2012 for offences including rape, trafficking and conspiracy to engage in sexual activity with children. Further investigations have led to additional prosecutions linked to historic child sexual exploitation across Greater Manchester. Judges described the offending as calculated, organised and profoundly damaging, recognising that many victims would carry lifelong psychological trauma.

Yet convictions answered only one question: the guilt of the offenders. They did not answer why children were repeatedly failed before those prosecutions ever reached a courtroom.

The official inquiries found that the primary problem was not an absence of legislation. The criminal offences already existed. Rather, agencies failed to recognise organised grooming, safeguarding procedures were inconsistently applied, intelligence was not always effectively shared and vulnerable children were too often judged instead of protected. Some reviews also concluded that concerns about community tensions influenced professional decision-making in certain cases, although they stressed that institutional failures were complex and involved multiple contributing factors.

Political debate over those failures continues today. Sir Keir Starmer has consistently defended his record as Director of Public Prosecutions, pointing to reforms introduced after the Rochdale prosecutions that encouraged prosecutors to focus more closely on suspect behaviour rather than relying heavily on assessments of victim credibility. Nigel Farage has repeatedly argued that institutional accountability remains incomplete and has called for wider national inquiries into organised child sexual exploitation.

Independent MP Rupert Lowe commissioned his own inquiry into grooming gangs, arguing that previous investigations had failed to provide full transparency or accountability. Lowe's report calls for mandatory recording of offender ethnicity, stronger criminal justice responses, improved national data collection and further investigation into institutional failings. While his inquiry does not carry statutory authority, it has become part of the continuing national debate surrounding organised child sexual exploitation and institutional responsibility.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan also faced criticism after asking for clarification during a London Assembly meeting about what was meant by the phrase 'grooming gangs' before responding more broadly on child sexual exploitation. The exchange became part of the wider political discussion over how public authorities describe organised abuse and communicate with victims and the public.

There have unquestionably been improvements since the original scandal. Greater Manchester Police has established dedicated child sexual exploitation capabilities, multi-agency safeguarding arrangements have been strengthened, inspection reports have recognised improvements in identifying vulnerable children and historic offenders continue to face prosecution years after their crimes. Those reforms are significant and should not be dismissed.

However, reform is not the same as accountability.

For many survivors, organisational apologies and revised procedures have never fully addressed the institutional failures identified by successive inquiries. Former Greater Manchester Police detective Maggie Oliver has repeatedly argued that child sexual exploitation remains a continuing threat and has warned against believing the lessons of Rochdale have been fully learned. She has consistently maintained that safeguarding depends not only on procedures but on professionals who are prepared to challenge assumptions, recognise organised exploitation and place children's welfare above institutional reputation.

Child sexual exploitation has not disappeared. Police forces across England and Wales continue to investigate organised grooming offences while offenders increasingly exploit social media, encrypted messaging platforms, online coercion and county lines criminality. Organised abuse evolves. Safeguarding must evolve with it.

The greatest lesson from Rochdale is not that Britain lacked the legal powers to prosecute offenders. It is that institutions repeatedly failed to use those powers when vulnerable children first asked for help. Children who should have been believed were doubted. Warning signs that should have triggered intervention were overlooked. Opportunities to prevent further abuse were lost.

Rochdale Borough Council has acknowledged profound institutional failings and apologised to survivors. Public bodies have accepted that serious mistakes were made, while successive reforms have sought to strengthen safeguarding and improve inter-agency cooperation. Those changes deserve recognition.

Whether they have fully restored public trust is another question entirely.

Justice cannot be measured solely by the length of prison sentences imposed on offenders. It is also measured by whether institutions learn from catastrophic failure, whether public officials accept responsibility when safeguarding collapses and whether every vulnerable child reporting abuse today can expect to be believed, protected and acted upon without hesitation.

Until survivors believe those standards have been achieved, and until the public is confident that institutional accountability carries meaningful consequences as well as organisational reform, many will continue to conclude that justice in Rochdale remains unfinished.

articles.title: Lives cut short: Remembering the young people lost on Rochdale's roads
articles.excerpt: A look at the tragic loss of young lives on Rochdale's roads since 2020 and the ongoing efforts to improve road safety across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Every fatal road traffic collision leaves behind grieving families, devastated friends and communities asking whether more could have been done to prevent another life being cut short.

Since 2020, a number of young people have tragically lost their lives on roads across Rochdale borough. While every collision has had its own unique circumstances, each has served as a stark reminder that road safety is not simply about statistics – it is about sons, daughters, brothers, sisters, classmates and friends whose futures were taken away far too soon.

One of the most heartbreaking incidents came in April 2025 when six-year-old Myra Tahseen died after being struck by a vehicle on Ashfield Road. Emergency services fought to save her, but she sadly died from her injuries. The tragedy prompted an outpouring of grief across Rochdale, with floral tributes left at the scene and specialist officers supporting her family while investigations continued.

Although fatalities involving children and young people are thankfully rare, they remain one of the leading causes of death for those aged between five and nineteen across the United Kingdom. Rochdale's own Joint Strategic Needs Assessment highlights that land transport collisions remain among the principal causes of death for young people and reports that the borough's rate of children killed or seriously injured on the roads is around 15 per 100,000 population.

Behind every fatal collision lies a complex combination of circumstances. Excessive speed, distraction, impairment through drink or drugs, failure to wear seatbelts, poor weather, inexperience and momentary lapses in concentration can all contribute to devastating outcomes. Road safety experts consistently stress that many serious collisions are preventable through safer driving behaviour.

Young drivers remain disproportionately represented in serious road collisions nationwide. Inexperience, overconfidence and risk-taking behaviour can all increase the likelihood of being involved in a collision, particularly during the first years after passing a driving test. Equally, young pedestrians and cyclists are among the most vulnerable road users, particularly near schools, residential estates and busy roads.

Greater Manchester Police's Serious Collision Investigation Unit continues to investigate every fatal collision thoroughly, examining witness statements, CCTV, vehicle data, road conditions and forensic evidence to establish exactly what happened. These investigations often continue for many months before an inquest is held, allowing families to receive answers and, where appropriate, criminal proceedings to take place.

Road safety is not solely the responsibility of drivers. Pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists and passengers all have a role to play in reducing risk. Simple decisions such as slowing down in residential areas, putting mobile phones away, wearing seatbelts correctly, using pedestrian crossings where available and remaining alert around schools can make a significant difference.

Across Rochdale borough, organisations continue to work together to improve road safety through engineering improvements, education campaigns, enforcement against dangerous driving and community awareness initiatives. Every serious collision provides lessons that can help prevent future tragedies.

For the families who have lost loved ones, however, those lessons come at an unimaginable cost. Birthdays go uncelebrated, empty seats remain at family tables and communities continue to remember young lives that ended far too soon.

The hope shared by police, road safety campaigners and residents alike is that by learning from these tragedies, encouraging responsible driving and remaining vigilant on every journey, fewer families will have to experience the heartbreak of losing someone they love on Rochdale's roads.

A taxi driver has urged colleagues across Rochdale borough to remain vigilant after describing a frightening encounter while waiting for his next booking near Littleborough railway station.

The driver said the incident happened shortly after completing an Uber journey from Rochdale Railway Station to a passenger drop-off in Littleborough. After finishing the fare, he parked on a nearby street opposite Littleborough Railway Station while waiting for his next booking.

According to the driver's account, a man described as a white British male aged between 35 and 45 approached the vehicle accompanied by a dog. The driver says the man opened the car door without permission before placing the dog inside the vehicle, along with a bag containing unknown items.

When challenged, the driver alleges the man became aggressive and attempted to damage the vehicle by striking one of the windows. Fearing for his safety, the driver immediately contacted Greater Manchester Police while remaining inside the vehicle.

The driver says the alleged aggression continued while he was speaking to police, prompting him to drive to a safer, busier location near Sainsbury's Local in Littleborough, where he waited for officers to arrive.

Police subsequently attended the scene, took a statement and dealt with the reported incident. Rochdale Daily has approached Greater Manchester Police to establish whether any arrests were made or investigations remain ongoing.

Following the incident, the driver shared his experience publicly in the hope of preventing something similar from happening to others working in the taxi trade.

He is encouraging drivers to avoid waiting for jobs in isolated streets where possible and instead use well-lit locations with passing pedestrians or nearby businesses. He also advises drivers to keep vehicle doors locked while waiting for bookings and to contact police immediately if they feel threatened.

Personal safety is an important consideration for taxi and private hire drivers, many of whom work alone at all hours of the day and night. Drivers frequently find themselves waiting for bookings in unfamiliar locations or transporting passengers they have never previously met. Industry organisations have long encouraged drivers to remain aware of their surroundings, keep communication devices readily available and report suspicious or aggressive behaviour promptly.

While incidents of this nature remain relatively uncommon, they serve as a reminder of the challenges faced by those working in the transport sector. For many drivers, particularly those working evening and overnight shifts, staying alert and choosing safe waiting locations forms an important part of their daily routine.

Anyone who witnesses criminal damage, threatening behaviour or any incident where someone feels at immediate risk should contact Greater Manchester Police on 999 in an emergency, or report non-emergency incidents by calling 101 or using the force's online reporting service.

articles.title: Norden's hidden gem: Manchester fine dining right here in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Forget the drive into Manchester. Stocco in Norden is proving that one of Greater Manchester's finest dining experiences can be found right here in Rochdale.

When people think of fine dining, they often picture Manchester city centre, Spinningfields or the Northern Quarter. But tucked away in the village of Norden is a restaurant quietly proving that you don't have to travel into the city for an exceptional dining experience.

Stocco, on Edenfield Road, has rapidly established itself as one of Rochdale's standout restaurants, combining contemporary Italian cuisine with stylish surroundings and attentive service that would not look out of place in one of Manchester's best-known dining districts.

Occupying the former Mezbaan site, the restaurant has transformed the building into a modern Italian-inspired venue featuring elegant interiors, a spacious cocktail bar, outdoor terrace seating and room for more than 100 diners. Free parking is available nearby, making it an attractive alternative to the expense and inconvenience of travelling into Manchester for a special meal.

The menu blends traditional Italian cooking with modern British influences, offering everything from freshly prepared pasta and seafood dishes to premium steaks, artisan antipasti and seasonal chef's specials. Ingredients are sourced from local suppliers wherever possible, while speciality products are imported directly from Italy to retain authentic flavours.

Whether you're looking for a relaxed lunch, an evening celebration, cocktails with friends or a romantic meal, Stocco offers a level of quality and atmosphere that many diners would normally expect to find much closer to Manchester city centre.

Its arrival has also helped strengthen Norden's growing reputation as one of Rochdale borough's premier destinations for independent food and drink. Over recent years, the village has developed a thriving hospitality scene, attracting visitors from across Greater Manchester, Rossendale and Lancashire who are increasingly discovering what local residents have known for years.

Since opening, Stocco has built a loyal following, with many customers praising both the quality of the food and the welcoming service. The restaurant has become a popular choice for birthdays, anniversaries, family gatherings and business lunches, while its stylish décor and contemporary feel have made it equally appealing for casual dining.

Perhaps one of Stocco's biggest advantages is convenience. Instead of battling Manchester traffic, paying city-centre parking charges or relying on trains and trams, diners can enjoy a high-end restaurant experience just minutes from Rochdale town centre.

For residents of Rochdale, Bury, Rossendale and the surrounding areas, it is another reminder that outstanding dining experiences don't always require a trip into the city. Sometimes, one of the region's best-kept culinary secrets is much closer to home.

So, the next time you're considering booking a table in Manchester, it might be worth looking north instead. Tucked away in the heart of Norden is a restaurant that delivers city-quality dining with village charm—making it one of Rochdale's true hidden gems.

articles.title: Why are so many taxis in Heywood licensed in Wolverhampton and other areas?
articles.excerpt: Many private hire vehicles working in Heywood display licence plates issued by Wolverhampton, Knowsley and other distant councils. Here is why the practice is legal, why it remains controversial and when an offence may be committed.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Heywood have increasingly been asking the same question: why are so many taxis driving around the town registered in Wolverhampton, Knowsley and other places?

For many people, the sight of private hire vehicles displaying licences issued by councils hundreds of miles away raises concerns about who regulates them, whether they are operating legally and who is responsible if something goes wrong.

The issue has become controversial across England, with local authorities, taxi trade representatives and residents questioning whether the current licensing system gives councils enough control over the vehicles regularly working in their communities.

Why is it controversial?

The debate centres on cross-border licensing.

Since changes introduced under the Deregulation Act 2015, private hire vehicles are no longer expected to work primarily within the area that licensed them. As a result, a driver licensed by Wolverhampton City Council can legally spend most of the working day carrying passengers in Greater Manchester, provided the vehicle and driver comply with the law governing private hire bookings.

Critics argue that the system has weakened local oversight. Drivers may work almost exclusively in Greater Manchester despite being licensed by an authority many miles away, while local councils have less direct control over drivers they did not licence themselves.

Residents may also be unsure which authority they should contact if they wish to make a complaint. Enforcement can become more complicated when several licensing authorities are involved, while different councils may apply different licensing policies and standards.

These concerns have been raised by local authorities across England for several years, with many calling on the Government to reform private hire legislation and give councils greater control over vehicles operating regularly within their boundaries.

Does that mean these vehicles are operating illegally?

No. Although the system is controversial, simply seeing a vehicle licensed in Wolverhampton, Knowsley or another authority driving around Heywood does not mean it is breaking the law.

Private hire licensing works differently from the licensing of traditional taxis.

Unlike a hackney carriage, which can be hailed in the street or wait on an official taxi rank, a private hire vehicle must be pre-booked through a licensed private hire operator before the journey begins.

A Wolverhampton-licensed vehicle seen driving through Heywood could lawfully be travelling to collect a passenger who has already booked, dropping off a customer, waiting for its next booking through an operator or app, or returning from a previous fare.

The licence plate alone does not indicate whether the vehicle is acting lawfully.

When would it become an offence?

The law is much clearer if a private hire vehicle accepts work without a booking.

A private hire driver cannot legally accept passengers who flag the vehicle down in the street, wait on designated taxi ranks or carry passengers without a booking that has first been accepted by a licensed private hire operator.

Those activities are generally reserved for licensed hackney carriage taxis.

If residents witness a private hire vehicle picking up passengers without a booking, licensing officers can investigate whether an offence has been committed.

Who is responsible for enforcement?

One reason the issue generates debate is that responsibility can involve several organisations.

The council that issued the driver's licence retains important regulatory powers and can investigate complaints or suspend and revoke licences where appropriate.

Greater Manchester Police can deal with suspected criminal offences, while local licensing officers may carry out roadside inspections and joint enforcement operations with other authorities.

Many licensing authorities now share intelligence and work together to improve enforcement across council boundaries.

Why Wolverhampton?

Wolverhampton has become one of the country's largest private hire licensing authorities.

Over recent years it has processed applications from drivers across England, meaning many vehicles operating in towns and cities far from the West Midlands legitimately display Wolverhampton licence plates.

The same principle applies to vehicles licensed by authorities such as Knowsley and other councils outside Greater Manchester.

The bigger debate

The growing number of vehicles displaying out-of-area licences has become a national political issue.

Supporters of the current system argue that it provides flexibility for drivers, supports competition and allows passengers to access transport more easily, particularly through app-based booking services.

Critics believe councils should have greater powers over vehicles that spend most of their time working within their communities, regardless of where those vehicles and drivers were originally licensed.

Successive governments have considered reforms to taxi and private hire legislation, but cross-border private hire work remains lawful under the current framework.

What should residents know?

For anyone wondering why so many vehicles in Heywood display Wolverhampton, Knowsley or other out-of-area licence plates, the answer is that the law allows it.

Their presence alone is not evidence of illegal activity.

The important legal question is not where the vehicle is licensed, but whether it is operating as a genuine private hire vehicle, with every journey properly pre-booked through a licensed operator.

Where there is evidence that a private hire vehicle is accepting passengers without bookings or otherwise breaking licensing rules, those concerns can be investigated by the relevant licensing authority and, where appropriate, the police.

Reservoir safety

Reservoirs can present serious dangers, even during warm weather. Although the surface may appear calm, the water is often significantly colder than expected, which can trigger cold water shock, rapid loss of muscle control and difficulty breathing.

Hidden hazards including steep underwater drop-offs, deep silt, submerged debris, strong currents around inlets and outlet structures, and rapidly changing water depths can also make self-rescue extremely difficult. Even experienced swimmers can quickly find themselves in difficulty.

United Utilities and emergency services consistently advise members of the public not to enter reservoirs for swimming due to these risks. If someone gets into difficulty in the water, members of the public are advised to call 999 immediately and avoid entering the water themselves wherever possible.

articles.title: Residents urged to attend Greenvale planning meeting as decision nears
articles.excerpt: Campaigners are encouraging residents to attend Rochdale Borough Council's Planning Committee as councillors prepare to consider the Greenvale planning application for land south of Greenvale in Bamford.
articles.content_html:
Residents opposed to the proposed Greenvale development in Bamford are being encouraged to attend next week's Planning Committee meeting, where councillors are expected to consider the application for housing on land south of Greenvale. Campaigners say a strong public turnout will demonstrate the level of local concern surrounding the proposal.

The application, reference 25/00405/FUL, is listed as Item 7 on the agenda for Rochdale Borough Council's Planning Committee meeting on Wednesday, 5 August. The meeting is scheduled to begin at 6pm, with the Greenvale application expected to be considered during the evening.

The appeal has been organised by the Bamford Green Belt Action Group and supported by the Save Bamford Greenbelt campaign, which has urged residents to attend the meeting regardless of whether they intend to speak. In a public appeal, campaigners said simply being present would help demonstrate to committee members how important the decision is to the local community.

Campaigners argue there remain significant planning policy and evidence gaps which should be addressed before any decision is taken. They believe the proposed development would result in the unnecessary loss of Green Belt land and have consistently maintained that the site should remain protected from development.

The Green Belt surrounding Bamford has been the subject of longstanding debate as Rochdale Borough Council seeks to balance housing demand with the protection of open countryside. Supporters of Green Belt protection argue the land plays an important role in preventing urban sprawl, preserving the character of existing communities and providing valuable green space for wildlife and recreation. Those in favour of development argue additional housing is needed to meet growing demand and support future economic growth.

Planning Committee members are required to determine applications based on planning law and adopted planning policy rather than the popularity of a proposal. Material planning considerations can include matters such as highway safety, flood risk, ecology, landscape impact, heritage, design and compliance with local and national planning policies. Issues such as the identity of an applicant or the level of public support alone are not determinative, although representations submitted by residents are taken into account where they raise relevant planning matters.

Residents wishing to observe the meeting can attend in person, while those who have registered in advance may be permitted to address the committee in accordance with the council's procedures. Anyone intending to speak should check Rochdale Borough Council's guidance on registration deadlines and speaking arrangements before the meeting.

The committee's decision will determine whether planning permission is granted, refused or deferred pending further information. Whatever the outcome, the decision is expected to be closely watched by residents across Bamford and neighbouring communities, where the future of Green Belt land continues to generate strong public interest.

articles.title: Middleton protest planned as organiser sets out bail conditions ahead of event
articles.excerpt: A protest is planned in Middleton Gardens on 8 August, with organiser Jamie Thomason outlining his intended arrangements and referring to bail conditions while police are expected to oversee the event.
articles.content_html:
A public protest is due to take place in Middleton Gardens on Saturday, 8 August, with organiser Jamie Thomason stating he intends to comply with his bail conditions while addressing supporters before leaving the area. According to a statement published on social media, Greater Manchester Police will have officers present during the event, with police liaison officers said to be aware of the arrangements.

In his announcement, Thomason said he would be joined by several guest speakers from across the UK, including Ashlea Simon of All for England, Dorothy Jones and Pag Billy UK, with additional speakers yet to be confirmed. He described his planned speech as being based on information which he says can be verified through publicly available sources and encouraged supporters to attend the demonstration.

Thomason also referred to his current bail conditions, stating that he is prohibited from congregating with more than ten people. He asked supporters not to approach him in groups, saying he had agreed with Greater Manchester Police that he would attend, deliver his speech and leave Middleton immediately afterwards. He also stated that he would give his speech from a distance and would not become involved in any confrontation because he did not intend to breach his bail conditions.

Rochdale Daily has not independently verified the specific bail conditions referred to in Thomason's post, and reports them only as claims made by the organiser himself.

The right to peaceful protest is protected in UK law under Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, although that right is subject to restrictions where they are lawful, necessary and proportionate. Police have powers under the Public Order Act 1986, as amended by more recent legislation including the Public Order Act 2023, to impose conditions on public assemblies where they reasonably believe serious public disorder, serious disruption, intimidation or damage may occur. Participants are expected to comply with any lawful conditions imposed.

Greater Manchester Police has previously stated that its role at public demonstrations is to facilitate peaceful and lawful protest while taking action where criminal offences are committed or where public safety is at risk. Depending on the circumstances, officers may deploy protest liaison teams, public order officers or other resources to manage events and minimise disruption to the wider community.

The planned demonstration is likely to attract differing opinions from residents. Supporters say the event is intended to raise awareness of issues they believe are affecting communities across the country, while others are expected to disagree with both the organisers and the views expressed. Peaceful disagreement and lawful protest are protected rights, provided they remain within the limits of the law.

Anyone travelling through Middleton town centre on Saturday should be aware that there may be an increased police presence around Middleton Gardens while the demonstration takes place. At the time of publication, no official road closures, dispersal orders or protest conditions had been publicly announced.

Rochdale Daily has contacted Greater Manchester Police for comment to confirm the policing arrangements for the event, including whether officers will be deployed, whether any conditions have been imposed under public order legislation, and whether any road closures, dispersal powers or other measures are anticipated.
